versions.body:
# Configuration Profiles and Multiple-Match Decision Record

Initially, profile selection and multiple-match results were discussed together because both pass through the command-line entry point. That classification now seems too coarse, but at the time we first needed to avoid a more direct problem: the command line should not maintain a separate rule hierarchy.

At the time, we started by examining the entry point at `src/ansiblelint/cli.py`. The file visibly has direct dependencies on argparse, logging, os, and sys. What can be confirmed is that the command line receives user input and orchestrates execution; the fact that these dependencies are all near the entry point does not make rule definition, match formation, and final display one responsibility.

There were two directions.

1. The command line expands the user-specified profile into a rule set, then passes the expanded result to the runtime;
2. The command line only stores the selection provided by the user, while the hierarchy is still interpreted on the configuration side.

The tentative choice is the second. The reason is not that the entry point cannot expand it, but that once the hierarchy appears in both places, a name change first shows up as a selection error and then as a change in the number of matches. During troubleshooting, this would conflate whether the parent relationship changed with what the user actually selected. The selection side should only pass along the selection; the rule side then decides what that selection includes.

Here, "configuration side" was only the responsibility label used at the time; it does not mean the command line takes no part in validation. The entry point still needs to read the arguments, retain the user's selection, and hand off the state required for execution. Not having it rewrite the hierarchy as a local branch is intended to make hierarchy changes independently checkable.

A weaker decision was also made for multiple matches: collect matches first, then apply filtering. Do not let a filter condition alter the preceding matching process. An object may relate to multiple rules; how many results the user ultimately sees is a later presentation concern. If filtering is made to look like matching too early, an empty result has no clear provenance: it may mean that no rule matched, or that a match was excluded afterward.

This ordering does not commit to a particular container type, nor does it require every rule to execute simultaneously. It preserves only one fact that can be discussed: matching and filtering are not the same action. If display, statistics, or exit status are adjusted later, there is no need to redefine whether a rule matched.

The profile name, parent representation, ordering within the collection, and display priority for results had not yet been decided. In particular, this cannot be used to conclude that strict mode and profile are the same thing; they merely both appear near the command line. Whether strictness affects rule selection or the interpretation of existing results has not yet been checked.

One question also remains unresolved: if the same object matches multiple rules and the user selects a narrower profile, are the unselected matches never generated, or are they generated and then not displayed? This draft contains no sample that can be reviewed, so "ends up empty" cannot stand in for an answer.

Continue with this division for now: the entry point retains the selection, configuration interprets the hierarchy, the runtime forms matches, and filtering is left to result processing. The next review should first find the existing selection entry point, then check which section processes the result set.
versions.change_summary: Recorded the initial division of responsibilities for the entry point and multi-match handling.

versions.body:
# Profile and Multiple-Match Decision Record

The initial draft recorded profile selection and multiple-match results side by side because both came into view near the command line. After review, that starting point is still retained, but "being in the same entry point" is no longer treated as a reason to assign them the same responsibility. The entry-point file `src/ansiblelint/cli.py` shows direct dependencies on argparse, logging, os, and sys; it provides a place to observe the argument flow, not a description of all runtime responsibilities.

## Tradeoffs Retained from the Initial Draft

There were two initial candidates.

The first was to immediately expand the profile name supplied by the user on the command line into the final rule list. The argument comes in, the name becomes a list, and the runtime afterward only consumes the list. This approach is short and makes a single invocation look as though it has one clear context.

The second was for the command line to store only the selection, with the hierarchy continuing to be interpreted by configuration and the runtime working from the selection and the existing hierarchy. The initial draft tentatively adopted the second option. The core reason was that the same parent-child relationship must not be stored in both the entry point and the configuration. If a hierarchy name changes, the expansion logic on the entry-point side and the definition on the configuration side may change at different times; when investigating a failure, it would not be possible to determine first whether the deviation came from the user selection, the hierarchy description, or rule execution.

This tradeoff does not mean the entry point has no work to do. It still needs to accept arguments, prepare the runtime state, and pass the selection to the downstream path. Retaining a selection is different from reinterpreting the hierarchy: the former preserves the user's intent in the invocation, while the latter copies knowledge of the parent into another location. The initial draft reduced this boundary to the sentence "the selection side should only pass along the selection" without spelling out its consequences.

Another judgment in the initial draft was that multiple matches should first be formed and then filtered. "First" here describes a logical order, not an implementation commitment about a list or generator. The same object may be associated with multiple rules, and the content ultimately shown to the user may also be filtered. If unwanted results are removed during matching, someone who later sees an empty set cannot tell whether no rule matched, a rule did not participate, or an existing match was removed during processing.

The initial draft specified neither result ordering nor that all matches had to be saved in one place. It only avoided writing the filter as the matcher. There were no real invocation samples at the time, so it also did not turn "multiple matches" into a seemingly precise result table.

## Counterexamples Found During Review

The review first looked for a counterexample to the idea that expanding at the entry point was the easiest option. Suppose the parent relationship in the configuration changes while the command line continues converting the name into a rule list in the old way. The parameters supplied by the user have not changed, but the rules being run may have. The logs would superficially look like a problem with argument parsing or selection handling, when the actual issue would be that the two pieces of hierarchy knowledge had not changed together. Conversely, if the entry point only retains the selection, a hierarchy adjustment can be reviewed independently on the configuration side; changes on the caller side do not need to prove their correctness through the result count.

This counterexample does not require moving all selection-related code out of the entry point. The boundary it draws is narrower: the entry point should not separately own the explanation of "which profile overrides which profile." Argument validity, whether the user explicitly supplied a selection, and what selection information the downstream run receives are still things to check near the entry point.

A more aggressive option was also compared at the time: have all rules produce results first, then remove unwanted matches by profile name. Its advantage is that every run follows one path, and temporarily viewing all results is easier. The review did not accept it as the default semantics because it conflates two types of empty result. A rule may not have participated in the run, may have participated without producing a match, or may have matched but not been shown; if all of these become "no results," statistics, troubleshooting, and exit-state decisions lose the distinction.

Therefore, a profile should not be understood as a terminal result filter. It is closer to pre-run selection information; filtering handles results that have already been formed. Both may jointly affect the output visible to the user in one invocation, but one decision should not substitute for the other.

## Old Assumption About Strict Mode

The initial draft placed strict mode next to the profile, and the review temporarily produced a working assumption: a broader profile could naturally produce stricter result determination, while a narrower profile would do the opposite. This judgment came from the arguments being adjacent, not from a behavioral check.

This section is now marked as deprecated. A profile answers which rules belong to a selection; strictness is closer to how existing diagnostics should affect the final state. Both may change the conclusion visible to the user, but neither can be derived from the other. If strictness is put into the hierarchy, whether a warning changes the state will look like a question of whether a rule was selected; if the profile is instead used to represent the exit policy, the same hierarchy will lose its stable meaning across invocations.

The old assumption is retained to explain why the issue was later split apart, not as a current rule. Parsing the parameters in the same place only means that the entry point needs to carry both; it does not mean they belong to the same hierarchy contract.

## An Incomplete Result Check

This review intended to use one multiple-match report to confirm the division of responsibilities: when the same object produces multiple matches, whether a change in selection takes effect before the run or after result formation, and where filtering affects what the user sees. No complete command or terminal output was left behind, so this attempt cannot be written up as completed validation.

What remained was a recurring disagreement over wording. One person described not seeing a result as "the rule did not match"; the other held that selection or filtering could still have occurred in between. The disagreement was not resolved by adding more terms. Instead, it left a recording habit: when describing a result, state the stage first. Whether a rule did not participate, participated but did not match, or matched but was no longer displayed cannot all be covered by the same phrase "no results."

Whether the collection needs stable ordering internally was not decided. There was also no material to rely on for whether different matches need the same priority. Filling these gaps with default behavior would cause a later implementation to treat undecided items as existing constraints.

## Review Marginal Notes

Two brief comments were left during review.

First: result count is not evidence of the profile hierarchy. Result count is affected by the input, rule participation, and subsequent processing; the parent relationship cannot be inferred from the count of a single run.

Second: the number displayed is not equal to the number of matches formed internally. Even if the user ultimately sees only one result, that does not establish that the other decisions never occurred. This comment does not require all matches to be displayed permanently; it cautions that the display layer cannot replace runtime facts.

Together, the two comments support a narrower decision: hierarchy interpretation, pre-run selection, match formation, and result processing need to be described separately. They may be adjacent in the code, but they cannot be compressed into one issue during review merely because they are adjacent.

## Tentative Decision

Maintain the division in which the configuration side owns the profile hierarchy, the entry point stores the selection, the runtime forms matching results, and the downstream stage performs filtering. Strict mode is removed from the profile discussion and left to be handled as a result-determination issue.

This review did not decide the final display order for multiple matches, nor whether selecting a narrower profile should leave a visible trace for rules that did not participate. The actual invocation entry point has not yet been added back; without that material, any conclusion based on empty output is not sufficiently reliable.

# Configuration Profiles and Multiple-Match Decision Record

This record has long been used to revisit two closely related questions that should not be merged: who defines the rule hierarchy, and who handles the case where a single run produces multiple matches. The earliest clue came from `src/ansiblelint/cli.py`. The entry file shows direct dependencies on argparse, logging, os, and sys, so it is easy to assign argument handling, rule selection, and result display to the same place. The judgment retained later was that this is suitable for observing how user input enters a run, but insufficient grounds for concluding that all runtime responsibilities belong to the command line.

The following preserves several sections written at different points in time. The early records contain misjudgments as well as checks that were not completed in time. They are no longer current operating instructions, but deleting them would make several later boundaries appear to have emerged from nowhere.

## 2023-06: Original Questions Near the Entry Point

The question at the time was not to first lay out a complete profile table, but to prevent the command line from maintaining a second copy of the rule knowledge. Two directions were discussed.

The first approach was to expand the profile specified by the user into the final rule list at the entry point, then pass the list to the runtime. The call chain is straightforward: arguments come in, names are converted into a list, and downstream code only consumes the list. In the short term, this would reduce the number of objects passed onward and make it easy to observe locally which rules ran in "this run."

The second approach was for the entry point to store only the user's selection, while the configuration continued to define the hierarchy, with the runtime continuing to work from the selection and hierarchy. The initial draft tentatively chose the second approach. The reason was not that the command line could not expand the selection, but that once parent-child relationships appear in both the entry point and the configuration, a name change will first appear as a selection error and may then appear as a change in the number of matches. During investigation, "what did the user select," "how is the hierarchy defined," and "which rules actually participated" would be forced into a single answer.

In the initial draft, "configuration side" was a responsibility label; it did not mean that the entry point should not perform validation. The entry point should still receive arguments, save the selection, prepare the state required for the run, and pass it to the subsequent path. The distinction is that saving a selection is not the same as reinterpreting the inheritance relationship. The former preserves the caller's intent, while the latter stores the hierarchy knowledge in two places.

The same initial draft also recorded a weaker decision about multiple matches: collect matches first, then process filtering. "Collect" here describes only the logical order; it does not commit to a particular container or a specific execution path. An object may be related to multiple rules; filtering conditions may determine which results continue to be presented or affect the final state. If filtering is prematurely disguised as part of matching, an empty result loses its provenance: it may mean that there truly was no match, or that a match was found and then excluded.

At the time, profile selection and multiple matches were placed on the same page because both affect the final output. This categorization was later considered insufficiently precise. A profile is pre-run selection semantics, while multiple matches are a result fact that may be formed after the run; appearing in the same invocation does not make them the same rule.

The initial draft did not decide the profile names, parent representation, display order, or result priority. Nor did it define the relationship between strict mode and profiles. At the time, it was only known that both appeared near the command line, which was not enough to conclude that strictness was part of the hierarchy.

## 2023-06: A counterexample in the review margins

The first round of review did not require moving all selection-related code out of the command line. The counterexample raised in the review was more specific: if the hierarchy exists only in the rule list expanded by the entry point, parent relationships on the configuration side and command-line behavior will change together. Even if the rules that ultimately participate remain unchanged, the first thing a reader of the code sees may be a change that looks like argument handling. As a result, hierarchy changes can no longer be reviewed on their own.

The boundary established by the counterexample was this: whether arguments are valid, whether the user has provided a selection, and which options must be carried into a run are still entry-point concerns; the entry point is no longer responsible for "restating which name inherits from which name." Once these two layers are separated, configuration changes can be checked first against hierarchy definitions, changes to invocations can be checked first for whether the selection is correctly preserved, and changes in result counts need not immediately be blamed on arguments.

The review also discussed another convenient approach: let all rules produce results first, then remove unwanted hits by profile name at the end. Its advantages are a uniform execution flow and the ease of temporarily inspecting all output. The problem is that it conflates "whether a rule participates in execution" with "whether a result is displayed." An empty set after filtering cannot indicate whether there was no match, no participation, or participation followed by hiding; if someone later uses result counts to determine status, empty results from three different sources will be conflated into one.

For that reason, profile was not defined as a final-stage result filter at the time. This decision did not require displaying all hits externally, nor did it deny that filtering could occur at the final stage. It only rejected using the same name to describe both pre-run selection and post-run display.

A short note was also left in the review margins: result counts are not evidence of hierarchy. This does not mean result counts have no value, but rather that inputs, rule participation, hits, and filtering all affect the count. The number of results returned by a single run cannot, on its own, prove a profile's parent relationship.

## 2023-11: The verification session was not completed

Someone subsequently tried to verify the division of responsibilities above using a multi-match report. The goal was narrow: when the same object has multiple hits, at which stage should a change in selection take effect, and at which stage should filtering affect what the user sees? The complete command, complete input, and complete terminal output were not retained from the session, so this attempt cannot be documented as a completed verification.

What was retained was that, during the discussion, some people directly described "not seeing a particular result" as "that rule did not match." Others disagreed, on the grounds that selection or filtering might still intervene. This disagreement was not resolved by adding a result table; instead, it prompted a recordkeeping practice: when describing a result, first state the stage it is at. A rule not participating, a rule participating but producing no hit, and a hit being produced but not subsequently displayed cannot all be covered by the same phrase, "no results."

This verification also did not decide whether stable ordering was required within the set. There was likewise no material to rely on regarding whether different matches needed the same display priority. Writing these unresolved items in as default behavior might appear to make the document complete, but would in fact pass undecided matters along as existing constraints.

In the records at the time, "collection" did not refer to any specific container implementation. It merely gave the discussion a common object: first acknowledge that there may be more than one match at runtime, then discuss which layer of results selection, filtering, aggregation, or status determination each deals with. Without this distinction between layers, any subsequent statistics could only be inferred backward from the final output.

## 2023-11: Abandoned strict-mode inference

The old draft placed strict mode right alongside the profile notes and proposed a working hypothesis: a broader profile could naturally lead to stricter result evaluation, while a narrower profile would do the opposite. This judgment came from their both appearing near the command-line interface, not from checking their behavior.

This passage was later explicitly overturned. A profile answers which rules belong to a selection; strictness answers how existing diagnostics affect the final status. Both may change the conclusion the user ultimately sees, but neither can be inferred from the other. If strictness is written as part of the parent relationship, whether a warning changes the status will look like a question of whether a rule was selected; if profile names are used to express exit policies, the same hierarchy will lose its stable meaning across different invocations.

The old judgment was not deleted because it explains why early discussions placed the two parameters in the same paragraph. What actually needed correction was not moving a parameter away from the entry point, but the order of explanation: first establish rule selection, then look at the results formed during execution, and only then discuss how those results affect the exit status.

At the time, someone also argued that if the user ultimately sees only one result, there is no need to retain multiple matches. The objection was not a demand to always display all results, but a point that the number displayed and the number of results formed internally are not the same concept. If later work requires statistics by tag, an explanation of the status, or simply an answer to why a particular result disappeared, merging too early loses the context needed to make that judgment.

This point also does not mean that every invocation must retain intermediate state at the same level of detail. It only emphasizes that if a subsequent judgment truly depends on where a match came from, that origin cannot be guessed retroactively from empty output on the spot. Whether to display results, how to aggregate them, and how to change the exit status should be explained separately, rather than replaced by a profile name.

## Archived old proposal: Treating names as result buckets

The following passage preserves an early proposal that no longer applies.

> After selecting a profile, matches unrelated to that name can simply be treated as nonexistent; this way, the terminal only needs to handle a result bucket that has already been narrowed down.

The problem with this wording is not that it aims to narrow the results the user sees, but that "treated as nonexistent" erases the distinctions between stages. It does not distinguish between a rule not participating, a rule not matching, and a result not being displayed. If someone later sees a difference between the statistics and the terminal output, this proposal also gives them no way to determine when that difference arose.

The old proposal had its context at the time: everyone hoped to handle selection and display through a branch near the entry point, avoiding the spread of the multiple-match problem to more places. It provided no real samples, nor did it specify the ordering, deduplication conditions, or status rules within the result bucket. It therefore cannot continue to serve as the default semantics.

Another old suggestion was to "observe how many results a single run returns and use that to verify the parent relationship." This also no longer applies. The result count varies with the input content, actual matches, and subsequent filtering, and cannot by itself prove an inheritance relationship. The hierarchy must be checked against its own declared relationships, rather than inferred backward from the number of outputs in a particular run.

## Responsibility boundaries viewed from the entry point

Tracing back from the entry point, the responsibility boundaries can be written more clearly than in the initial draft. The command line reads user input, prepares the selection, and passes the state required for execution to downstream paths; configuration provides hierarchy information; rule execution produces a hit for each rule; only the result-processing stage deals with filtering, aggregation, and the final state.

This does not require every layer to become an independent module, nor does it mean that a function can interact with only one object. It is a review order. If a change adds a hierarchy name, first check the configuration definition; if a change alters how the user's selection is carried, first check the entry point; if a change alters how many diagnostics an object produces, first check rule execution; if it only changes output or exit determination, it should not be misreported as a hierarchy inheritance issue.

This division of responsibilities explains why multiple matches must not be swallowed by the profile name. Even if a selection ultimately causes some rules not to participate, the remaining rules may still produce multiple hits for the same object. Filtering can determine which hits continue outward, but it should not borrow the profile's name to conceal its own judgment.

The entry file remains the starting point for tracing parameter flow. It is not the sole place that explains multiple-match behavior. When the selection appears correct but the result count does not match expectations, first distinguish whether the rules participated, then whether hits were formed, and finally examine filtering and state; do not classify every judgment as a command-line issue merely because the parameter names appear in the same file.

## Two concerns left in the meeting excerpt

One concern was that the hierarchy might gradually turn into a series of command-line aliases. If the entry point both accepts the selection and remembers which names a given name is equivalent to, the documentation and implementation will preserve different relationships, and later it will only be possible to guess who overrides whom from the result count. The review inclination was to make parent relationships part of the configuration contract, with the entry point only accepting and carrying the selection.

Another concern was that the earlier filtering happens, the easier it is to lose explainability. The side supporting early filtering argued that hits users ultimately cannot see are not worth continuing to collect; the opposing side pointed out that not being displayed eventually does not mean that it did not occur at runtime. The meeting did not require retaining all intermediate information without limit; it only required not allowing the filter to replace the matcher.

The meeting stopped at two unresolved items: the stable display order for multiple matches had not been decided, and the priority among all filters had not been decided either. They require real invocation samples, but there were no samples that could be archived at the time. Preserving this pause is more faithful to the circumstances than filling in a seemingly precise set of outputs.

## Correction trail

First correction: the original statement that "because the parameters are handled together, their semantics can be merged" does not hold. Sharing an entry point only shows that they are parsed in the same invocation; it does not show that profile, filtering, and exit determination belong to the same contract.

Second correction: the original approach of "running all rules first and then deleting results by profile" is no longer the default. It conflates whether a rule participates in execution with whether its result is displayed, and creates ambiguity for empty results.

Third correction: the original assumption that "strictness can be derived from the breadth or narrowness of the profile" no longer applies. Strictness and hierarchy selection overlap, but they answer different questions. The former handles how existing results affect state; the latter handles which rules belong to a selection.

The parts that were not corrected also include the following: the approach of forming hits first and then processing filtering remains. It does not promise every runtime detail, but it remains the necessary order for distinguishing multiple matches from filtering. If someone infers the execution process only from the final output, this order should still be checked first.

## State diagram for discussion

The diagram below only expresses the decision sequence used throughout this page, not specific function calls or result containers. Selection enters execution first, and matches are produced after execution; filtering and status interpretation come after matches. Sorting and priority are not included in the diagram, because neither has been decided by this page.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Selection
    state "User selection" as Selection
    state "Rule hierarchy interpretation" as Hierarchy
    state "Rule execution" as Execution
    state "Multiple matches" as Matches
    state "Filtering and aggregation" as Filtering
    state "Result determination" as Outcome
    Selection --> Hierarchy
    Hierarchy --> Execution
    Execution --> Matches
    Matches --> Filtering
    Filtering --> Outcome
    Outcome --> [*]
```

"Hierarchy interpretation" in the diagram does not exclude the command line. It simply prevents the entry point from redefining parent-child relationships. "Filtering and aggregation" also does not mean that all results must be processed in the same place; it means that filtering at the end cannot be retroactively described as the reason a rule never matched.

## 2025-03: Current agreement

After the layers of records above, the current agreement is recorded here, rather than written back into the paragraph from 2023: CLI and the configuration share an ordered PROFILES contract: the key order is min, basic, moderate, safety, shared, production, each entry uses extends to indicate inheritance, min has no parent and production inherits from shared;--profile writes a single-element profile selection,--strict only promotes warning-only results without disrupting clean success.

This convention tightens the wording in the initial draft that "configuration owns the hierarchy." The early records did not specify the hierarchy order or explain how the root node and parent levels should be represented; these details now belong to the same public contract. `min` is not an alias temporarily derived by the entry point, and `production` is not a result set assembled by the presentation layer. The hierarchy is described by the `extends` relationship in `PROFILES`, and the entry point preserves the user-provided single selection through `--profile`.

The order here is also part of the contract, rather than a way to make the output look tidy. When reading the hierarchy, the smallest root level must be identifiable first, followed by the later selections through the declared parent relationships. Scattering names across entry-point branches or inferring relationships from the number of results would reintroduce the ambiguities already exposed by the early records.

The boundary of strict mode is fixed here as well. `--strict` handles determining the result of warning-only, without changing the meaning of success when there is no diagnostic. It should not instead become a parent condition for the profile, nor should a profile name be used to infer whether it is active. This keeps the selection rules and the interpretation of existing diagnostics open to separate discussion.

The current convention does not claim that all issues with multiple matches have been resolved. It only defines what the profile hierarchy does not handle: profiles are not responsible for fabricating or erasing match facts, strict mode is not responsible for redefining the hierarchy, and filtering should not be used to explain whether a particular rule participated in execution.

## Boundaries that multiple matches must still follow

For multiple matches, this page preserves a narrower decision rather than a complete presentation specification: first acknowledge that multiple hits may be produced at runtime, then discuss which layer of results selection, filtering, aggregation, and status determination each addresses. This order ensures that multiple hits for the same object are not incorrectly interpreted as never having occurred merely because the user ultimately sees only one.

When selecting a narrower profile, rules that did not participate must still be distinguished from results that participated but were not displayed. The former is an effect of pre-run selection; the latter is processing after hits have been formed. Both may reduce the final output, but they are not the same kind of change. This distinction cannot be skipped when discussing result counts.

If statistics by label are needed later, first specify whether the statistics cover raw hits, filtered results, or final displayed results. In simple scenarios, the three may be the same; with selection and filtering, they may not be. The statistical basis should not in turn change the profile's inheritance relationship, nor should it require one output to prove selection, matching, and presentation simultaneously.

Likewise, the number of results displayed in the terminal does not validate parent relationships. The terminal is one end of result processing, while the hierarchy is specified by the configuration declaration. Two objects may happen to produce the same number of results in one run, or may produce different numbers because their inputs differ; these phenomena cannot replace a direct hierarchy check.

## Matters still left aside

The actual invocation entry point for multiple matches still needs to be added back. The existing material only points out the need to verify the results seen by the user and does not retain complete inputs and outputs. Therefore, this page cannot specify a stable display order for multiple hits, nor can it assert that all filtering occurs at the same layer.

Another related issue is when to aggregate. Collecting matches before filtering does not automatically answer which set aggregation should operate on. If new result-statistics requirements arise later, we first need to clarify whether they are intended to describe what happened during rule execution, the filtered results, or the content the user ultimately sees. This issue should still not retroactively change the profile inheritance contract.

On the entry-point side, there is also an ongoing issue with the order in which things are read: when you see a parameter change, first confirm whether it changes how the selection is passed along or how the hierarchy is defined; when you see a change in the result count, first confirm what happened separately in rule participation, match formation, and filtering. Collapsing these judgments back into a single command-line branch often only recreates the earlier confusion.

## Appendix of Retained Old Examples

**Old example one: treating profile names as result buckets.** An early draft assumed that once a name was selected, all matches unrelated to that name could simply be treated as nonexistent. This example is now outdated: it did not distinguish between a rule not participating and a result being filtered out, nor could it explain why statistics and display might later differ. It is still retained here to show how "selection," "match," and "display" were once collapsed into a single concept.

**Old example two: using result counts to verify parent relationships.** The draft once suggested observing how many results a run returned to determine whether one profile covered another profile. This example is also no longer applicable. Result counts vary with input, rule matches, and subsequent filtering, and cannot by themselves prove an inheritance relationship; parent relationships should be checked through the declarations in `PROFILES`.

**Old example three: strictness follows the breadth of selection.** This was once the inference most likely to arise around the entry point: a broader selection scope should produce a stricter final status. This inference was later withdrawn because it collapsed pre-run rule selection and post-run result evaluation into a single condition. It is retained to remind readers not to mistake parameters appearing side by side for a semantic binding.

None of these old examples comes with reproducible input, so they cannot be treated as current test cases. What they preserve is the path of misinterpretation at the time, and why the discussion now needs to be broken down by stage first. The current agreement has tightened the semantics of the hierarchy and strict mode; the specific ordering of multiple matches, display priorities, and actual invocation examples still need to be added separately.

# Jinja-compatible interface adjustment proposal

The initial draft discusses rule identity and task error context separately. The existing whitespace check retains a historical name, and the boundaries among the configuration entry point, diagnostic ownership, and file implementation are unclear. If the name is changed directly, ignore entries in old configurations may no longer take effect; if the old name is kept entirely, the new expression check will remain constrained by the old scope.

There are currently two directions: retain the old name as the public identity and add more granular diagnostics internally; or establish a new public identity for the rule and use the old configuration name as a compatibility entry point. The first has lower migration cost, but callers still have to infer the match category from the message text. The second requires configuration conversion, but separates identity from the specific diagnostic.

Start by checking `src/ansiblelint/rules/var_spacing.py`. The file header shows `re`, `sys`, typing declarations, and `AnsibleUnicode`, confirming that this involves expression text and YAML string objects. This alone cannot determine the public interface, nor can it establish the complete fields of the task error object.

The second direction is preferred. Whether the source object is retained and how callers display it still need to be confirmed separately.

# Jinja-compatible interface adjustment proposal

After one review, the option of retaining the old name as the sole public identity was set aside. Although it would not require users to update their configurations immediately, it would put expression format, invalid structure, and historical variable whitespace under the same old label, so callers still could not reliably distinguish match categories. The new approach first establishes a caller-facing identity, then interprets the old configuration as compatibility input.

Verification remains limited to `src/ansiblelint/rules/var_spacing.py`. This contains regexes, system modules, type declarations, and `AnsibleUnicode`. These local details support conclusions about text handling and input types; they do not support including task structure, YAML categorization, or the complete error-message format in this design. The filename should not become the new public name.

## Trial scope

The new identity should cover Jinja expression-format checks, rather than continuing to limit the scope to variable whitespace. The old `var-spacing` configuration remains a compatibility entry point and, after parsing, feeds into the new granular diagnostics. This gives old ignore entries a migration destination, and the results do not need to maintain two public names at the same time.

Expression fields and implicit-expression fields cannot use the same fix. Ordinary expressions can be handled according to their delimiters; `when` is already in an expression position, so fixing whitespace must not unconditionally add template wrapping. Record this as an interface constraint for now; specific examples and error context have not yet been included in the review findings.

Narrow task error context separately to source attribution. Do not splice the rule name into the message, and do not change the expression-rule message just to add task information. If the result object can retain the source rule, the caller Fang Ke can append the task location in its own presentation layer; the required fields have not yet been decided.

The rollback conditions are that compatibility input cannot be reliably mapped to the new diagnostics, or that an implicit expression is changed into text with template wrapping. If either occurs, first restore separate handling for the old entry point; do not treat the message text as a fallback interface.

# Jinja Compatibility Interface Adjustment Proposal

This proposal started with a filename and only later split apart two issues that are easy to conflate: what the Jinja check should be called for callers, and how the result object should carry provenance when a task error occurs. The former affects configuration migration and diagnostic filtering; the latter affects whether the presentation layer can add task context. They can be reviewed in the same round, but they cannot be handled with the same message format.

An earlier option was to keep using the old name as the sole entry point and explain its new meaning in the output text. Its cost became clear during review: the old label in the configuration and the new category in the result had no stable boundary, so callers could only infer ownership from the wording. Adding another expression diagnostic later would also require expanding this historical name. The option remains documented, but is no longer the migration strategy.

The point of reference for verification is `src/ansiblelint/rules/var_spacing.py`. The only adjacent references visible at present are `re`, `sys`, `TYPE_CHECKING` in typing, `Any`, `Dict`, `List`, `Optional`, `Union`, and `AnsibleUnicode`. This shows that the processing code handles both regex text and YAML string objects. It is enough to support this proposal's discussion of the rule interface and formatting fix, but not enough to establish the full structure of the task object, and that path should not be expanded into a YAML classification entry point.

## Interface Chosen to Keep

The public identity is fixed as a single rule ID; the sublabel expresses the category of check that matched. Legacy configuration continues to support compatibility parsing, but once parsing is complete it resolves only to the current identity, rather than exposing both the old and new names as results callers must compare. Configuration migration is therefore input-side work, while diagnostic presentation reads the stable identity and sublabel from the result.

The public rule ID of JinjaRule is jinja; the compatibility mapping for legacy var-spacing and the expression-whitespace diagnostic both use jinja[spacing]. The sublabel of check_whitespace is spacing, and when is treated as an implicit expression, so enabled == true remains without template braces.

This boundary has a practical consequence: "add template delimiters to all expressions" cannot be used as the repair rule. The value of `when` is already a conditional expression; the fix is whitespace around the operator, and the field's expression form must not change as a result of formatting. Ordinary expressions continue to be handled according to their own input boundaries; this proposal does not use that distinction to add a new YAML processing responsibility.

The compatibility mapping also cannot leave only an alias during configuration loading and then expose both identities in the output. A user's original legacy configuration must be able to resolve to the current granular diagnostic, while the result returned to the caller should have a single rule ownership. If a legacy entry cannot complete this resolution, that is a migration failure and should not be concealed by rewriting the diagnostic wording.

## Task error context enrichment

The decision on error context is narrower than in the earlier proposal. The `MatchError` produced by the rule retains the `rule` attribute, so the source rule object is passed to the caller with the result. The expression rule does not splice the task location, display name, or other task context into the error body; the presentation layer can decide, based on its own object relationships, whether to append that information. This also avoids inferring the source through string matching.

This round makes no commitment to the field list for task context. The proposal only identifies the source rule object as something that can be passed through; it does not freeze the task name, location, or error-body format. If more fields are genuinely needed later, they should be discussed as a separate object change rather than treating the compatibility mapping as an implicit context channel.

## Trial, Failure, and Rollback

During the trial, first check three independent outcomes: whether legacy configuration can parse to the current granular diagnostic; whether the expression-whitespace fix preserves the original boundary of the implicit field; and whether the result object lets the caller retrieve the source rule. The third check covers object ownership only; it does not require the caller to adopt any particular display wording. If any one of these does not hold, adding explanatory text cannot make up for the missing interface.

On rollback, restore separate handling for the legacy entry and remove exposure of the new identity before it is stable. If the implicit expression is wrapped in template braces, roll back the formatting-fix branch; if error context can only be obtained by concatenating text, do not ship it with this change. Keeping legacy configuration readable is a migration condition, not a reason to keep exposing the legacy result identity.

What remains undecided is which fields task context will need in the future and which layer the caller will use to present the rule source. These questions do not affect this round's local choices about the public identity, the compatibility entry, and the `MatchError` source attribute; nor should they be written as completed task examples.

# NameRule Exclusion-Path Troubleshooting Tree

When name-related results don't match expectations, don't change YAML yet. The initial triage split into only two questions: did the input reach rule processing, and is the object being checked a task or a play? If these two questions aren't separated, it's easy to record no result as a missed rule report, or to write up a play issue as a task issue.

Start by reviewing from `src/ansiblelint/rules/unnamed_task.py`. The file is adjacent to `AnsibleLintRule` and `Lintable`, which makes it useful for confirming the object received by NameRule; it is not the overall entry point for loading YAML. A path name containing unnamed does not by itself mean that all results are related only to tasks missing names.

```text
Name-related result anomaly
|
+-- File did not enter checks
|   `-- Record the input shape and exclusion, then stop at the entry point
|
`-- File entered checks
    +-- Object is a task
    |   +-- No name
    |   `-- Has a name; still retain the original text
    +-- Object is a play
    |   `-- Record separately; do not mix it with tasks
    `-- Object unclear
        `-- Add the object record first; don't infer from the result text
```

There was an unverified working assumption at the time: `unnamed-task` in the old configuration only affects display and does not change filtering. There is no counterexample yet, so don't change the configuration based on it. When encountering old records, retain the original label, object type, and whether the file was excluded; if any one of these is missing, don't attribute the result to the name rule.

Another boundary remains unresolved: when the task filename is used as a prefix, is the name obtained from the path the same as the name shown to the user? During troubleshooting, don't manually strip the part that looks like a prefix. Save the original name and file location first, then verify against the rule side later.

A note next to the draft says: if a file has no result, don't directly write "name has already passed." No result may simply mean that the input didn't reach the rule.

# NameRule Exclusion-Path Troubleshooting Tree

For name-related anomalies, don't start by guessing the cause from the diagnostic text. First determine whether Lintable sends the file into rule execution, then distinguish whether the object is a task, play, or import_playbook item. Early records collapsed these cases into "unnamed"; review found that this classification masks differences in entry points and also prevents filters in the old configuration from lining up with current results.

The entry point should still be traced back from `src/ansiblelint/rules/unnamed_task.py`. The file contains type declarations such as `AnsibleLintRule`, `Lintable`, and `TYPE_CHECKING`, `Any`, `Dict`, `Union`, `Optional`, and others; this is suitable for checking the boundary between the rule object and the input object, but not for inferring the entire YAML classification chain from the filename. This page only covers procedures for cases where name diagnostics and exclusion paths are adjacent; it does not fold in the behavior of other rules.

## First confirm whether the input reached the rule side

When similar content produces a name hint in one place but nothing at all in another, follow the branch below first. No result by itself is not a diagnosis and cannot be treated directly as a pass.

```text
No name result
|
+-- Is the file excluded by Lintable?
|   |
|   +-- Yes: record the exclusion status and input form, then stop attributing the cause to the name
|   `-- No: continue identifying the object
|
+-- Is the input a play, task, or import_playbook item?
|   |
|   +-- play / import_playbook: go to the play-name record
|   `-- task: go to the task-name record
|
`-- Cannot identify the object?
    `-- Supplement the input record; do not infer the object from the result text
```

"Excluded" here only means that Lintable did not hand the input over for execution by this round of the rule. It is not an assessment of whether the name is valid. Exclusion occurs before the rule runs, so a single missing result cannot prove that the name meets the requirements; likewise, do not bypass the exclusion path just to obtain a name result. When comparing, record the affected unit and a nearby unchanged unit in the same run, because they may differ only at the entry point, not in the name field.

An earlier procedure was written as "add the name first, then rerun." This wording remains in the old records but is no longer suitable for use. It conflates whether the file participates in execution with whether the name content needs to be checked. If the input has already been excluded, adding a name, changing capitalization, or changing the display text cannot prove whether the name rule has a problem.

## Old labels are not an independent branch

The initial draft treated old name labels still visible in the configuration as a separate category of rule result. This made them convenient to search for in old reports, but caused two practical problems: missing task names and missing play names were mixed together; and the configuration filter syntax could not be matched item by item with the labels in the new results.

The side note at the time was:

> When you see an old label, filter by the old category first; if you cannot find the object, then inspect the name rule.

This procedure has been deprecated. Old labels may still be used as search entry points for historical configurations and reports, but troubleshooting must first confirm which type of object and which name check the label is associated with. Keeping only the single word "unnamed" is not enough to determine whether to look at a task, a play, or the file entry next.

After the second review, the operational record was fixed to retain three items: object category, original label, and whether it was excluded by Lintable. The original label is used to locate the old configuration; the object category determines the name branch; and the exclusion status determines whether the process should stop before the rule. Only when all three pieces of information are kept together can an entry-point problem avoid being miswritten as a rule problem.

## A name being present still leaves branches

The `name` field in a task or Play mapping is where the name rule reads the name. The field being present does not mean the check is finished. The earliest records recommended "skip the name rule as long as a name exists." This simplification was not retained because it collapsed field existence, field content, and object type into the same judgment.

Once a name exists, at least three related cases remain: checking the name's initial letter, checking the prefix derived from the task filename, and checking the template location. They cannot be merged simply because they all appear as name issues. The initial-letter branch examines the name content; the prefix branch requires the task filename and configuration template; and the template-location branch requires knowing where the template appears.

In one temporary reproduction, the troubleshooter first deleted the portion at the beginning of the name that looked like a file prefix, then compared the remaining text. This approach was later rejected: it could not show whether the prefix itself satisfied the configuration, and it also compressed different task files into identical samples. The current record keeps the original name, task filename, and prefix template, rather than using manually stripped text as a substitute for the input.

`{stem}` is placeholder notation in the prefix template, representing the portion of the task filename after its extension is removed. It is not the YAML field, nor is it a generic variable to be manually replaced in the troubleshooting record. When this prefix is involved, first retain the original name and corresponding file; if the prefix does not match, do not skip this branch and attribute the issue directly to capitalization.

Templates also need to be recorded separately. Braces in a name do not necessarily indicate an empty-expression issue; the name rule cares about where the template appears. When a template is found, first record where it occurs in the name, then decide whether to continue checking the name rule. Do not send the issue to another rule merely because of the braces.

## Stopping points adopted after review

During review, someone proposed returning one result for all objects without names to shorten the decision path. The proposal did not pass. The input boundaries for tasks, plays, and import_playbook items differ, so a unified result would prevent subsequent records from explaining where the object came from; and objects that already have names may still enter other name branches.

The operational steps were therefore changed to:

1. Starting from the anomalous file, confirm whether Lintable excludes the input.
2. If it is excluded, retain the input form and exclusion status, then stop; do not continue modifying the name content.
3. If it is not excluded, confirm whether the object is a task, play, or import_playbook item.
4. If the object has no name, check where the old label is used in the historical configuration, but do not treat the old label as an independent current branch.
5. If the object has a name, check the initial letter, prefix template, and template location separately.
6. If the object, entry point, and field are all clear but the result still cannot be explained, trace back from the adjacency between the rule object of `unnamed_task.py` and `Lintable`.

The unresolved question is whether the external aggregation should leave the name status as "not checked" after the input is excluded. The current review can only establish that the exclusion path precedes rule execution; it cannot decide the aggregation behavior.

# NameRule Exclusion Path Troubleshooting Tree

When name diagnostics are missing, old tags still appear in the configuration, or only some similar files produce results, do not modify the rules or add names yet. Record separately whether the file passed through Lintable, what type of input object it is, whether the mapping contains a name field, and the final diagnostic text. This record has been revised several times: the old draft treated excluded inputs as missed reports, mixed missing play names into task issues, and mistook old compatibility tags for independent rules.

The entry point is still `src/ansiblelint/rules/unnamed_task.py`. Visible direct neighbors include `AnsibleLintRule` and `Lintable`, and the file header also contains type declarations such as `TYPE_CHECKING`, `Any`, `Dict`, `Union`, and `Optional`. It is useful for confirming where the name rule connects to input objects; do not reduce all name-related behavior to "unnamed tasks" just because the path contains unnamed.

For new anomalies, start with this tree. Stop points in the tree only mean to stop attributing causes on this page, not that the anomaly has been resolved.

```text
Name results are anomalous, or expected results do not appear
|
+-- Is the file excluded by Lintable?
|   |
|   +-- Yes
|   |   +-- Record the input form and exclusion path
|   |   `-- Stop: do not continue looking for results on the name-rule side
|   |
|   `-- No
|       |
|       +-- Is the object a play or a import_playbook item?
|       |   `-- Enter the play-name branch
|       |
|       +-- Is the object a task?
|       |   |
|       |   +-- Name field missing: retain the old configuration syntax, then check the missing-name branch
|       |   +-- Name present but initial letter anomalous: check the capitalization branch
|       |   +-- Prefix check enabled: first verify the file-derived prefix
|       |   `-- Template in a restricted position: check the template-position branch
|       |
|       `-- Object still cannot be identified
|           `-- Stop: add input-object records, do not infer the object from tags
|
`-- File and object are both clear, but the results still cannot be explained
    `-- Revisit the connection between the rule object and Lintable
```

## 2023-05-24: The Initial Brief Account

The earliest field notes had only two implications: trace name issues from `unnamed_task.py`; when there was no result, first confirm whether the rule had been invoked. At the time, the samples on hand were concentrated on task mappings, and the records did not separate the file entry point, object category, and name content. For a small number of tasks, this framing seemed sufficient, but it later left behind a series of "unnamed" records that were very difficult to reproduce.

One working assumption in the initial draft was that `unnamed-task` in the old configuration affected display only and would not change filtering. There was no counterexample at the time, so it was not recorded as a firm conclusion; but when old reports were read later, many people misread this sentence as meaning that old labels could be ignored. This section is retained to explain why the early records kept only the labels and not the objects.

The same initial draft also phrased "no name result" as if it were nearly equivalent to "no problem with the name." This is not a reliable equivalence. No result may come from the file entry point, or it may be because the object was not confirmed; an empty result alone cannot determine whether to change the name, change the configuration, or return to Lintable first.

The simplified routing used at the time was as follows, but it can no longer be used on its own:

```text
No name result
├─ Add name and run again
└─ If there is still no result, inspect the rule
```

It did not ask whether the input had already been excluded, nor did it distinguish between a task and a play. If an old reproduction only records "disappeared after adding a name," it can now be treated only as a clue that entry-point information needs to be added, not as proof that a particular name branch has already been established.

## 2023-year initial draft's margin note on the duty page

After the initial draft, a very short reminder was added in the margin of the duty page: first record whether the file entered the check. This addition did not provide complete exclusion criteria, nor did it attempt to explain the YAML classification chain; it merely blocked the most common misjudgment of the time before the name rule.

The exclusion path here refers to the case where Lintable did not pass an input to this round of rule execution. It is not an assessment of the file's content, nor another way of saying that the name is correct. When the file does not enter the rule, adding a name, changing the initial letter, or replacing a piece of display text cannot make this round's result explain the name rule itself.

The duty log recommended retaining two pieces of original information: the form in which the input appeared, and the fact that it was on the exclusion path. Then stop at the entry point. If it is necessary to continue investigating why the file did not enter the check, verify it separately through Lintable's entry path; forcing the entry-point issue into the name branch will make the next troubleshooter think that the rule can determine whether the file is checked.

A conclusion often written down at the time was:

> The file was skipped, so there is no problem with the name.

This wording is no longer used. It turns a judgment that the rule had no opportunity to make into a conclusion. Current records only state that the file was not handed to this round's name rule, leaving the as-yet-unexplained entry-point issue where it is.

## 2024-01-29: Review samples split "unnamed" apart

Review began with differing results from similar content: one place showed a name hint, while another had no name result at all. Someone initially planned to compare two name fields, but after looking at the records, discovered that the two inputs had not first been confirmed to have gone through the same entry point. The review order was therefore changed to check Lintable first, then the object category, and only finally the fields and results.

This round did not attempt to enumerate every possible exclusion condition. What can be confirmed is that exclusion occurs before the name rules run, so a single resultless case cannot prove that the name meets the requirements; likewise, the exclusion path should not be bypassed just to obtain a name diagnostic. If the affected unit and an adjacent unchanged unit can both be retained, that is more useful than retaining only one "anomaly YAML": the two may differ only at the entry point, not in the name field.

The review also pointed out that "unnamed" cannot continue to serve as the sole object description. At a minimum, task, play, and import_playbook items must be separated first. When the object is unclear, the diagnostic text cannot be expected to identify the object. When an old report contains only a label and no object, add the object record first; if it cannot be filled in, leave it as an unconfirmed old sample.

The record format established at the time was not complicated: object category, original label, and whether it was excluded by Lintable. The original label helps locate the old configuration; the object category determines which name branch to enter; and the exclusion status determines whether this page should continue checking the rules. If any of the three is missing, the conclusion can easily turn into a guess.

## 2024-01-30: Deletions and edits on the review page

During the review, someone suggested streamlining the process: task mappings with a name field would simply skip the name rules, while objects without a field would all return one result. This approach appears to reduce the number of branches, but it cannot explain cases where an object still falls into other name checks after a name exists, and it would also collapse play and import_playbook items into task handling.

The review did not adopt this proposal. Whether the field exists, the field contents, the object type, and the file entry must be judged separately. If objects are first folded together by field, the later initial-letter, file-prefix, and template-location checks will lose their source; if they are first folded together by result text, play anomalies will be swallowed by task anomalies.

The review excerpt is retained below:

> Do not infer the object from the old label; obtain the object first, then interpret the label.

This sentence remained on the page afterward, not to replace the rule description, but because it can prevent one specific error: seeing an old label, immediately looking for a particular task, and then recording an object that was not found as a filtering failure. The old label can still be used to search historical configurations, old comments, and old reports, but it should not become the current branch detached from the object.

The same round of review also corrected the statement that "name fields belong only to tasks." The name rule reads the `name` field in a task or Play mapping, so when the field is present, the object category must still be confirmed first. This correction does not mean that all objects have the same structure; it prevents troubleshooting records from flattening the input source.

## Reproduction 2024 years later: Manual prefix stripping failed

After the task filename was included in the name-prefix check, a temporary reproduction used a manual stripping approach: it deleted the segment of the name that looked like a prefix and compared only the first letter of the remaining text. The sample looked very straightforward at the time; it was later discovered that this deleted the content that most needed to be checked—the prefix itself, whether it matched the configuration, and which task file the original name came from.

The old recommendation read:

> Extract the task name after the first delimiter; text before it does not participate in the investigation.

This recommendation is deprecated. It collapses different task files into the same remaining string and gives the prefix branch no opportunity to be recorded. When this prefix is encountered, retain the original name, task filename, and prefix template; do not use the manually processed string as the only input.

`{stem}` is placeholder notation in the prefix template, representing the part of the task filename with its extension removed. It is not an ordinary field in YAML, nor is it a variable to be replaced arbitrarily during troubleshooting. Once prefix checking is enabled, first verify the relationship between the template and the task file. If this layer has not yet been clarified, do not skip it and directly conclude that the issue concerns the first letter of the name.

This is also why the early "look at lowercase first" order was later changed. A name may begin with a portion derived from the filename, so the investigator must first distinguish whether the check targets the complete name or the remainder after the matched prefix has been removed. The old records only said "the first letter is inappropriate" and did not retain the template or file information, so they can only help explain why the attribution was too hasty at the time.

## Follow-up reproduction in 2024: the template is not an alias for a whitespace issue

When curly braces appear in a name, people previously redirected the issue straight to expression-whitespace troubleshooting. That switch was too broad. Here, the name rule is concerned with where the template appears in the name; expression formatting concerns a different kind of content processing. The two phenomena can occur near the same content, but the presence of curly braces alone cannot be taken to mean that they are the same issue.

An old margin note read:

> If there is a template, check the expression first, then return to check the name.

That margin note is no longer used as an operational step. Its remaining value is to explain why some historical records conflated template position with formatting. When reading such old records, first restore the file entry point and input object; if the file has already been excluded, stop at the entry-point record; if the object still cannot be determined, stop at the object record. Do not fabricate parsing conclusions based on curly braces.

The template-position branch must not swallow the prefix branch either. A name may have a file-derived prefix and may also have a template; the troubleshooting record needs to state what was confirmed first, rather than putting every name containing curly braces into one broad category.

## 2025-04-25: Returning from compatibility misclassification to entry-point order

The most recent review began with "no result and the old tag was still searchable" and was initially classified as a compatibility issue. After the cross-reference records were completed, the affected file was found to be on an exclusion path in Lintable, and the name rule had received no input. This finding did not establish any specific exclusion condition, nor did it expand into a broader file-classification conclusion; it only corrected the attribution order.

Since then, this page has explicitly recorded the stopping points:

- File excluded: retain the excluded path and input form, and stop checking the name rules.
- File not excluded but object unclear: first identify the task, play or import_playbook item, and stop guessing the object from the result text.
- Object clear but name field missing: then proceed to the record for a missing task name or missing play name.
- Object clear and name present: proceed to the initial-letter, prefix, and template-position checks separately.
- Entry point, object, and field all clear but result still unreasonable: return to the boundary between the rule object in `unnamed_task.py` and `Lintable` to recheck.

"Stop" does not mean closing the issue. For example, whether an excluded file should display some status in an external summary is still an adjacent issue; but it cannot be answered by continuing to modify the name rules. The on-site record should state which layer the investigation stopped at, so follow-up verification does not restart from the wrong branch.

## Current recording procedure

When a new anomaly is added to this page, save the original input first, and do not immediately add a name or remove a prefix just to reproduce it. After confirming that Lintable has not excluded it, confirm the object. Tasks, plays, and import_playbook items must not share a single record just because they all involve names. When the object is unclear, do not guess what it is from the diagnostic text; first add the object record.

When a task has no name, check whether historical configurations, old comments, or filter conditions still contain an old label. It can continue to serve as text for locating old material, but it cannot serve as an independent category detached from the task object. When a play has no name, stay in the play branch; do not close it by relying on a task record. When a name exists, confirm the initial letter, prefix template, and template position separately, and retain the original name.

If the issue occurs in only one file, record that file's entry status and object category. If adjacent unchanged units can serve as a comparison, retain them as well; do not rewrite different objects into identical YAML fragments just to produce a uniform sample. Rule-side review takes place only after the entry point, object, and field are all clear.

## Current naming convention

After the routing above, interpret diagnostics according to the current convention: the public ID of NameRule is name: a missing task name uses name[missing] and is compatible with unnamed-task, casing uses name[casing], a missing play name uses name[play] and outputs All plays should be named., prefixes use name[prefix] and {stem}, and a template in the middle uses name[template].

This convention applies only to name results that have already entered the rule and whose object category has been confirmed. It cannot be used to evaluate files excluded by Lintable, nor can it be used in reverse to select the input category when the object is unclear. Name text, object boundaries, and file entry points each retain different information, and on-site records should not collapse all three back into a single "unnamed" conclusion.

## Adjacent items not yet split out

Whether external summaries need to retain an "unchecked" name status after a file is excluded by Lintable is still not decided here. This page only requires that this situation not be recorded as a rule pass or a rule failure. If further work is needed, add material at the boundary between exclusion paths and summary behavior, rather than continuing to adjust name labels.

Another point to investigate is whether any entry points in historical configurations still filter only by old labels. When one is found, first record its usage location and object category; do not rewrite all old configurations at once on this page. The old wording is still part of the migration trail.

## Old Appendix: Reproduction Method No Longer Recommended

The following procedure comes from early field investigations and is retained for those who need to understand old reports:

1. Find an input with no name.
2. Temporarily add a name field.
3. If the result disappears, record the original anomaly as a name rule issue.

This reproduction method has been deprecated. It did not first confirm whether the input had passed through Lintable, nor did it distinguish between tasks and plays; a result disappearing after a name change does not establish which name branch produced the original result. When a historical record says only "disappeared after adding a name," treat it as a clue that still needs entry point and object information, rather than as an established conclusion.

There is also an even earlier handwritten note beside the appendix: "Filter by the old labels first, then find the object." This is likewise no longer recommended. It is useful for understanding how old reports were aggregated, but it cannot replace the object, entry point, and prefix information added later.
