# YAML Rule Compatibility Migration Guide

## Entry Points Left by the Old Records

This page originally used `src/ansiblelint/rules/playbook_extension.py` as the starting point for investigation. The reason was practical: the issue names and call names in the old records all pointed here, and the file header also contained `Lintable`, `MatchError`, `List`, and `os`. So the early migration sequence was to find the YAML entry point first, then find play handling, and finally examine how rules were dispatched. This sequence was not proven to be the complete call chain, but it was indeed the easiest path to recheck in the old version.

Early drafts also described "YAML with tasks" and "YAML with rules" as two possible ways to identify an entry point, without saving the classification result as an object property. Inline noqa was also recorded only as a generic type of comment. Complete outputs from successful and failed calls were not retained at the time, so these two statements cannot serve as descriptions of the current rules.

## The Method Retained During Review

The second review split the migration into two parts. First, check the kind determined from the content itself, then check the line-level skip information left by parsing; before dispatch, also check the skip tag on the play or task. The old method was to trace back by file location and start again from the entry point whenever results were inconsistent. This method was slow, but it could distinguish "inconsistent classification" from "rules did not execute."

Old configurations may also contain `# noqa` without a colon, followed directly by a rule tag. Another form is `# noqa: <rule-tag>` on a task line. The old records did not distinguish the two, so migration cannot consist solely of string replacement; at a minimum, retain evidence of how each form entered the task's skip information. To roll back, first restore the mapping between the old configuration and the old entry points, then check whether the same line is still treated as the original skip entry. Do not override it with a new global switch.

## Classification and Ordering Corrected Later

When checking this contract now, classification is based on top-level content: a generic YAML containing `tasks` goes through `playbook`, and a generic YAML containing `rules` goes through `rulebook`. What is retained here is content-based classification, not filename-based classification. The corresponding parse result must retain skip entries with exact line numbers in `line_skips`; when rule dispatch reads a play or task's `skip_ansible_lint`, it skips that object before executing the applicable rules. When parsing encounters a fatal error, subsequent rules do not continue, and `stop_processing` in the result is set to true.

```text
before  path or suffix -> inferred kind -> rule dispatch
after   tasks -> playbook; rules -> rulebook
recheck    line_skips -> skip_ansible_lint -> stop_processing
```

Lintable classifies generic YAML as playbook or rulebook based on top-level tasks or rules, respectively; comment parsing writes # noqa: tags into the exact line_skips, a task or play's skip_ansible_lint skips rules before dispatch, and a fatal parse error sets stop_processing to true.

This revision also affects error mapping. A rule-generated `MatchError` still retains its source rule object through the `rule` property, calling Fang Ke to attribute the match to a specific rule rather than having to infer it again from the text. If `skip_ansible_lint` is attached to a play, it skips the rules applicable to that play; if attached to a task, it skips the rules applicable to that task. Both occur before rule execution and must not be conflated with stopping after a parse failure as a single outcome.

## Old Passages Retained Across Migration Batches

The first batch still located objects by file location, which was suitable for investigating old issues but not for determining the actual kind of YAML. The second batch added content checks but verified only the normal parsing path; the stopped state on the failure path was not consistently recorded at the time. Only the third batch stored classification, line-level comments, object-level skips, and fatal parsing separately. The old passages were not deleted because historical callers might still use them as an entry-point index; the statement that "seeing playbook_extension.py means entering playbook handling" is now outdated.

If the post-migration result only shows that no rules matched, first check whether the content actually belongs to `playbook` or `rulebook`, then check whether `line_skips` corresponds to the original line, and finally check whether the object carries `skip_ansible_lint`. If parsing has already failed, do not continue using the rule match count to determine whether skipping took effect; check `stop_processing` first. This sequence of checks narrows the old fallback method rather than removing the old path from the knowledge base.

Still missing are a complete set of successful/failed output comparisons and migration examples for old configuration tags across all call entry points. DOC-13 remain the reference location for this history; when you need to inspect the public return shape, go to DOC-14.

# Rule Return Shape Experiment Log

This pass starts by looking outward from `src/ansiblelint/rules/__init__.py`. The file header directly contains `copy`, `glob`, `importlib.util`, and `inspect`; it is both the entry point for the rule set and a suitable place to continue checking traces of dynamic module loading. First, record the return values, help text, and result statistics together to avoid later conflating objects from different layers based only on rule names.

Keep two small checkpoints on the input side. An YAML entry with no kind specified that contains `tasks` should be handled according to the playbook; the name check reads the `name` field from the task or Play mapping. That field is not the same observation object as rule ID: the rule itself can be called `name`, while the diagnostic details still come from the mapping content being checked.

The confirmed interface boundaries are as follows. The public shape of the rule runtime remains stable: MatchError exposes the source and effective tags through rule and tag, and custom rule help reads {module_name}.md; Lintable.data synchronizes the cache for the same object, AnsibleLintRule.matchtasks returns a flat list, BaseRule._order determines the order before ID, MatchError.lintable preserves the source object as-is; App.count_results records effective tags such as sample[failure] and sample[warning] through tag_stats.

Statistics records should not infer tags from terminal display text. The key for `tag_stats` should be the matched effective tag, so when `sample[failure]` and `sample[warning]` appear in the same result, retain their counts separately; the source rule object is kept on MatchError by `rule`. This way, callers do not need to guess again which rule produced the match.

The dynamic-module thread has not yet been documented as a loading order. # Nested Jinja Syntax Decision Record

The core judgment retained in v1 remains unchanged: Nested Jinja rejection and Specific syntax error taxonomy can be seen in the same test material, but they are not the same issue. The initial draft only said "shared entry point, separate judgments." That was enough at the time to prevent the two titles from being merged directly, but it did not explain how to use this boundary during review, nor why the test file is worth retaining while still being unable to determine ownership.

This review first retracts the old convenient shorthand. When searching through `test/rules/test_nested_jinja_rule.py`, it is easy to arrive at a natural-seeming explanation: since the filename contains nested Jinja, the samples, rejection behavior, and specific syntax classification should all be consolidated in one place. This explanation mistakes navigation for a conclusion. A file may be the earliest place found, and it may also contain tests for multiple adjacent phenomena; none of this is enough to show that every phenomenon shares the same implementation boundary.

## The Two Retained Decision Dimensions

The Nested Jinja side deals only with the relationship between input shape and rejection scope. The concern here is whether some content is rejected during checking because of nested delimiters, and whether new samples expand, narrow, or clarify that scope. The presence of an error description in a sample does not automatically give this side the authority to name an error category.

The specific syntax error side deals only with whether the error presentation is sufficiently distinguishable. Here, "specific" does not mean that the error text is longer, nor does it mean that the test name is more detailed. A taxonomy record has substance only when the actual output can distinguish a generic failure from a particular syntax issue. Conversely, an assertion that "input failed" can support a rejection judgment but may not support any taxonomy conclusion.

This distinction does not artificially split a continuous process. The two things may happen sequentially during one check, or may be triggered by the same input; the decision in this document only requires maintenance records not to describe this co-occurrence as a necessary causal relationship. Rejection of the input does not automatically imply that a stable specific classification has been established; a more detailed error does not automatically imply that the rejection scope for nested delimiters has changed.

## Recording Methods Not Adopted

**Merge them into one rejection error.**

The easiest initial approach was to treat nested input as the cause and the specific syntax error as the output of the same failure, and therefore maintain only one conclusion: "nested Jinja failure." This would reduce indexing and match the first impression provided by the test path. The problem is that it cannot express local changes: if only which inputs should be rejected is adjusted later, the old error presentation may still apply; if only the distinguishability of the error changes, the rejection scope may remain completely unchanged. The merged history would describe the two types of changes as synchronized, so this approach is not adopted.

**Retain only the rejection conclusion.**

Another conservative approach is to record only that "nested input should fail" and not address error classification. This does avoid prematurely assigning a name when the material is incomplete, but it would erase Specific syntax error taxonomy from the history. The next time material appears that can distinguish error presentations, readers would still return to the same entry point, but there would be nowhere to determine whether it supplements the old conclusion or opens a separate issue. This option is also not adopted.

**Fix the classification names first, then backfill with samples.**

This approach appears to provide a neat interface first and allow tests to be added gradually. However, the verifiable content currently points clearly only to the test entry point and its directly adjacent objects; it does not provide a complete set of classification items that can be fixed in advance. Writing the names first would merely force later samples to conform to early guesses. Once it became clear that the names came from the issue title rather than the actual error presentation, the cost of revision would be higher. Therefore, taxonomy is not treated as a naming exercise that can be completed a priori.

What is retained is the third approach: one verification entry point and two independent recording lines. When a sample involves both dimensions, the same revision note may state two observations in parallel, but it must identify which sentence belongs to the rejection scope and which belongs to the error presentation. When the material supports only one dimension, the other remains unchanged.

## Meaning of the Review Entry Point

The direct imports visible in the file are as follows:

```python
from pathlib import Path
import pytest
from _pytest.fixtures import SubRequest
from ansiblelint.file_utils import Lintable
```

These imports indicate that the review will encounter path handling, test execution, fixture requests, and `Lintable` content objects. They are sufficient to explain why this file is suitable as an entry point for samples and assertions: readers can continue from the test body to see how the input is constructed, how fixtures participate, and where the content objects are used.

They do not constitute another decision. The presence of `Path` cannot show how error locations are preserved; the presence of `pytest` and `SubRequest` cannot show at which layer diagnostic classification is formed; and the appearance of `Lintable` at the import site cannot by itself prove that it is responsible for rejection rules or error taxonomy. The previous tendency to describe these adjacencies as "the test file owns the error classification" is explicitly abandoned in this revision.

A more practical way to read this is to treat the path as an entry point to the issue, not as an ownership map. When reviewing Nested Jinja rejection, first inspect the input shape and corresponding assertions in the test body; when reviewing Specific syntax error taxonomy, first inspect whether the assertions or error artifacts actually preserve distinguishable semantics. Both review paths can start from the same file, but they do not have to end at the same object.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> entry
    state "Test verification entry" as entry
    state "Nested Jinja rejection" as nested
    state "Specific syntax error taxonomy" as taxonomy
    state "Separately recorded conclusions" as record
    entry --> nested
    entry --> taxonomy
    nested --> record
    taxonomy --> record
    record --> [*]
```

The arrows in the diagram indicate which decision line the material is assigned to in the record; they do not indicate runtime execution order. The two lines start from the same entry point to preserve their relationship during lookup; they remain separate before entering the record to prevent material from one side from supplying the conclusion for the other.

## Current Decision

1. Nested Jinja rejection independently describes whether inputs involving nested delimiters fall within the rejection scope. It does not absorb all adjacent Jinja issues, nor is it responsible for naming specific error classifications.

2. Specific syntax error taxonomy independently describes whether the error presentation has sufficiently distinguishable semantics. A classification conclusion is added only when an assertion, error object, or actual output supports this distinction. A bare failure result or filename is insufficient to complete this step.

3. `test/rules/test_nested_jinja_rule.py` is the current verification entry point. Future revisions may continue to use it to locate samples and fixtures, but they may not infer runtime ownership from the path alone, much less describe test adjacency as a public error interface.

4. Mixed samples are recorded in parallel. If a sample reflects both nested input and error presentation, it should separately state the information it provides for the rejection judgment and the classification judgment; when it reflects only one of them, only the corresponding part is updated. This way, someone adjusting the rejection rules does not also have to commit to the error interface, and someone adjusting the error presentation does not have to rewrite the meaning of all nested inputs as a side effect.

## Accepted Costs

Separate recording adds one more judgment: did the new material change the input scope, or did it change the error presentation? Maintainers may also see the same test entry point in both records. This duplication is intentional because it makes the intent of a change easier to recover than collapsing the two contracts into a single statement such as "nested expression failed."

Old material cannot be upgraded automatically either. A record that only says "nested expression failed" can continue to serve as a clue about the rejection scope, but it cannot be polished into a claim that a specific classification has been established. Conversely, even if a piece of material contains what appears to be a detailed error description, it must first be confirmed that this is the actual presentation rather than the test filename, issue title, or the author's summary during investigation. The historical wording may remain, but the categorization must be reassessed.

This does not require every change to add two completely independent sets of samples. One sample can serve both review paths, provided that the assertion makes clear what it proves. What must truly be avoided is turning "seen in the same place" into "the same object is responsible," and then carrying that speculation forward as a constraint on subsequent changes.

## Content Still to Be Added

The current material does not provide the complete taxonomy names, the number of categories, or stable boundaries for each category, so this record does not fabricate a list. The next addition should not be another inference from the path name, but a concrete assertion in the test body or an artifact that shows how the error is presented. If only boundary samples for nested input are obtained, update the rejection line; if only error material containing a source location or fine-grained category is obtained, update the taxonomy line.

`Lintable`'s actual use in this test file is still worth examining. It may help explain how content objects enter the check, or it may only be responsible for construction; until the test body has been read, this point should not replace the judgment on either side. This unknown does not affect the current decision; it only determines whether the next review should focus on input construction, fixture usage, or error assertions.

# Operator Formatting Trial Plan

This record retains the original split: operator formatting and a clean-run summary are related changes, but neither can substitute for the other. An early draft grouped both under "output consistency," which was too broad. Formatting touches expression content; the summary only presents results after rule execution. Follow-up investigations should check separately whether inputs were rewritten and whether results were summarized correctly.

`test/rules/test_nested_jinja_rule.py` was the regression entry point recorded at the time. It directly uses `Path`, `pytest`, `SubRequest`, and `Lintable`. This only establishes that the existing tests have nearby support for file inputs and request fixtures, not that this file covers every Jinja branch. The early proposal treated it as the home for all formatting behavior. That assessment was inaccurate; the original judgment is retained here to prevent this path from being mistaken for the overall entry point later.

## Formatting Approaches Considered at the Time

The first approach was to add spaces around operators in the text. It could quickly make simple `{{ foo + bar }}` look consistent, but there was no reliable way to tell whether `-` was binary subtraction or a negative sign in an index, or whether `~` was a prefix or a concatenation operation. Rewriting the text before guessing its semantics would likely introduce new differences on repeated processing.

The second approach was to use token positions and adjust adjacent whitespace only where a binary operator could be identified. The cost of this approach was having to preserve the original expression boundaries and hand text that could not be classified consistently back to the existing path. It did not promise to "format all Jinja," nor did it treat nested delimiters as fixable input.

Several counterexamples should remain guardrails during the trial. The canonical form for a negative array index should remain `{{ foo[-1] }}`; the negative sign must not be split out as an ordinary operator. A prefix tilde should remain `{{ ~a }}`; when a prefix tilde immediately follows a binary plus, the expected form is `{{ a + ~'b' }}`. These examples are not intended to expand the scope of autofixing, but to rule out the text-replacement approach.

The first draft also missed implicit expressions. Conditions in the `when` field should not be wrapped in additional Jinja braces when spacing is adjusted; for example, `enabled == true` should remain the condition itself. This constraint makes the "serialize first, then format" candidate unsuitable, because it can easily lose the field context.

## Original Summary Idea and Revisions

The initial idea was to use the same success message at the end whenever a run had no problems. This did not distinguish diagnostic counts from exit policy, and did not address warning cases. It can serve as a candidate for the clean path, but should not be treated as the established convention for all of CLI.

The target that can currently be verified is narrower: when there are no diagnostics, the success summary starts with `Passed with` and includes `0 failure(s), 0 warning(s)`. This is only a constraint on result presentation; it does not imply that runs with warnings must use the same structure, nor does it replace strict-mode checks. Using the summary string directly to determine failure would couple reporting and control flow again and should be avoided.

Leaving the exit status unspecified at the time was deliberate. Observations of a clean directory need to cover the exit code, whether any files changed, and whether any leftover directories remain. If any of these differs, the final line of output alone cannot establish that the trial succeeded. An earlier version treated "no diagnostics" and "no side effects" as equivalent; that judgment no longer applies.

## Trial Arrangements from This Round

For formatting, start with the shortest real sample from the existing tests. Once a sample is attached to ALR-207, it can be used to check whether processing it once and processing it again produce the same result; the sample itself should not be expanded into a complete rule design. If the result still depends on guessing the context, choose not to fix it rather than adding another global replacement.

For the summary, observe only clean runs. Check in this order: first confirm that the command finishes normally, then check the exit code, then check the working directory for unexpected changes, and finally verify the ending summary. This avoids letting polished output hide leftover directories or an abnormal status.

Rollbacks should also follow the two tracks independently: if formatting changes the existing handling of nested or ambiguous expressions, remove the autofix; if the summary needs to read rule details to construct a success result, roll back the shared summary change. The two changes do not have to ship together.

Open items remain: the fixture boundary provided by `SubRequest` in this test group has not yet been added to this record; it is also unconfirmed whether the cleaned-up working directory covers all Lintable input forms. These are no longer recorded here as blockers. If more samples are added through this test entry point, first confirm what the fixture actually does.

# Decision on Content Classification and Installation Detection

The boundary established in the initial draft still holds: Content-based kind inference should not be written up as a flow that goes straight from reading YAML to an installation prompt just because it was discussed alongside the Install-method decision hook. There was no reliable reproduction at the time; separating the two issues first was intended to prevent tentative guesses about content from being carried over into subsequent environment detection.

However, the old draft made `src/ansiblelint/yaml_utils.py` sound like a candidate location for handling both issues, and that claim needs to be narrowed. The review verified only the entry points on the YAML side and the direct dependencies in the file headers: `functools`, `logging`, `os`, `re`. They explain why the investigation started here, but do not show that this module determines the installation method. The old draft is being retained so that later readers do not mistakenly assume that deeper call relationships had already been traced at the time.

## Trade-offs Retained

The first approach was to continue using the file source, extension, or existing call location as the primary basis for classification, adding content inspection only when necessary. This would be easy to integrate into the old entry points, but if the same generic YAML came in through different locations, its category could change with the entry point. That cost conflicts with the goal of "determining the category from content", so this was not chosen as the final direction.

The second approach was to perform a single overall environment check that produces both the content category and the installation method. This initially looked tidy: callers would retrieve just one result, and all subsequent branches would reuse it. The problem is that the two sides read different objects. Content classification deals with structures already present in YAML; installation detection deals with the installation source at runtime. The former should not carry the environmental meaning of the latter, nor should the latter be inferred from the content object.

The decision is to retain two separate boundaries. A YAML entry without an explicit kind is classified as `playbook` when its content contains `tasks`; it is classified as `rulebook` when it contains `rules`. The installation method is still obtained through `config.guess_install_method` on the configuration side, and the version update check then determines how to handle the prompt. This does not require the YAML utility module to call this hook; rather, it rejects presenting the hook's result as part of content classification.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "YAML entry" as yaml_entry
    state "No kind specified" as inferred_kind
    state "Installation method detection" as install_decision
    state "config.guess_install_method" as config_hook

    [*] --> yaml_entry
    yaml_entry --> inferred_kind: No kind specified
    inferred_kind --> playbook: Contains tasks
    inferred_kind --> rulebook: Contains rules
    yaml_entry --> explicit_kind: Kind specified
    [*] --> install_decision
    install_decision --> config_hook
```

The two starting points in the diagram are deliberately not connected. It records the division of responsibilities at the time, not the execution sequence: a single CLI run may involve both content reading and version prompts, but that does not justify combining the two determinations into one return value. Explicit kind values are still handled using the existing explicit information; this record does not replace that with content inference.

## Answers the Review Did Not Establish

ALR-211 records the observation that the Content-based kind output could not be reliably reproduced. It can serve as a starting point for revisiting classification, but must not be read as confirmation of a single root cause. In particular, this round did not provide enough material to settle precedence rules when the same entry has multiple structural clues; showing `tasks` and `rules` as two separate observation paths in the diagram does not establish their priority when both are present.

ALR-228 records abnormal behavior in the Install-method decision under a particular usage pattern, and calls for checking the working tree and cache locations before and after execution. This check remains an incomplete observation and should not be retroactively rewritten as "the cache was modified". The boundary of the installation-method hook can be established first, while any side effects before and after the hook still need to be confirmed separately.

There was also an earlier idea to save effort: since both issues were being finalized in the same round, call Fang Ke to obtain a shared result and reduce wiring. This was rejected after review. The content side needs to distinguish reliably between `playbook` and `rulebook`; the environment side needs to retain an independent source for the installation method. Sharing an object merely to pass one fewer parameter would instead make category changes look like installation-method changes, or cause installation differences to be misdiagnosed as differences in YAML parsing.

This decision still includes the starting points from the old investigation, so it is useful for explaining why the two issues were not merged. Inline suppression metadata and per-label result statistics belong to a separate round of interface discussions, retained in DOC-21. If ALR-211 later provides reproducible conflicting inputs, only add conflict handling for content classification; if the working-tree and cache checks in ALR-228 produce results, then revise the installation-detection side.

# Proposal to Adjust Inline Suppression Statistics

Following the review, we first need to withdraw a premature preference in the initial draft: we cannot make suppression metadata a public result field just because it appears to belong to an individual diagnostic. Rule execution, filtering, and statistics may each read this field; if it is only added back at the outermost layer, the results callers see will be disconnected from the original matches. Per-tag result statistics also cannot be assessed solely by the final counts. The review needs to answer two questions first: where suppression information is attached to a result, and whether statistics are collected before or after filtering.

## What This Review Actually Covers

The starting point for verification is still `src/ansiblelint/rules/__init__.py`. The index only identifies it as an existing Python module for code reading and checking historical behavior. The file header includes `import copy`, `import glob`, `import importlib.util`, and `import inspect`; these dependencies place it near object copying, file discovery, dynamic loading, and checking, but they do not establish that this file owns all aggregation responsibilities. The field structure must be confirmed against the actual returned objects and existing call sites.

The maintenance entry-point updates for ALR-212 now serve as navigation, but they do not replace interface examples. We are not treating the maintenance actions in the card as evidence of results, nor drawing conclusions from caller feedback that has not yet arrived.

## Two Candidate Approaches

**Approach A: Results carry metadata.** Each rule result retains the minimum information associated with that instance of inline suppression, and the statistics layer reads the same set of results and aggregates by diagnostic tag. The benefit is that provenance for failures, unsuppressed results, and suppressed results can still potentially reside on the same object, allowing investigations to trace back to the original match. The risk is that adding attributes will change how callers compare, serialize, or display result objects; if existing callers treat the object as having a fixed structure, all consumers will bear the compatibility cost.

**Approach B: Keep results and statistics separate.** Leave the original result objects unchanged as far as possible, and carry suppression metadata and tag counts in an enclosing return structure. The benefit is that existing objects remain more stable, and experiments are easier to roll back locally. The risk is that the two structures need to be linked back together by position or identifier; once rule results have been filtered, statistics and details may each be missing an item, making it difficult for callers to explain why a particular tag appears in the counts.

This round does not declare either A or B the final interface. Keep "metadata ownership" and "statistics stage" as separate variables first, rather than trying to solve both problems with one field structure. If only one thing can be done initially, prioritize retaining internal records that show the difference before and after filtering; without that difference, the meaning of the per-tag counts cannot be determined.

## Verification Order

Start at the module entry point and locate the sections that create, copy, and return rule results. Record the object structure before it enters filtering. Then find where inline suppression is parsed and confirm whether it produces rule tags, line positions, or some other internal marker. Do not add speculative fields here, or treat search terms such as `skipped_rules` as confirmed return keys.

Then hold the input fixed and observe the results with no suppression, with one tag matched, and with multiple tags matched. Use successful calls only to confirm the default structure of empty results and the statistics container; failed calls must retain diagnostic details, not just totals. If the two types of call return different nesting levels, record the difference rather than forcing them into one structure. Each observation should answer just one question: whether the metadata can still point back to the original result, whether the statistics change after filtering, or whether existing callers can still read the original results.

Finally, use an input containing an unknown tag to see where it fails. Do not automatically group unknown entries under "other," as this would hide differences in tag spelling or parsing stages; this proposal does not define a new error type either. The interface owner needs to confirm whether callers want the raw tag, the normalized tag, or both.

## Compatibility and Rollback

Public changes should be split into two steps. The first step only adds internal records, without changing existing result fields or serialization structure; use these records to confirm the lifecycle of suppression metadata and the stage at which statistics are collected. Only in the second step should we choose A or B, while preserving a read path for existing callers. If the first step finds that metadata has already been lost after rule execution, the statistics layer must not fabricate it; the proposal falls back to retaining minimal provenance information at the parsing stage. If new fields cause existing callers to consider results unequal, roll back the field extension and use an enclosing statistics structure instead. If statistics can only be obtained from the filtered set, the documentation must explicitly call them "counts of remaining results," not the total number of original matches.

## Still Undecided

- The minimum fields and lifecycle of suppression metadata are undecided.
- Whether per-tag statistics cover original matches, filtered results, or both side by side is undecided.
- There is no evidence yet as to whether multiple rule tags preserve input order.
- The check of which result attributes existing callers depend on is not yet complete.

For the next review, bring back only the actual returned objects, one successful sample, and one failed sample. If these three items cannot be obtained, this page remains a set of candidate approaches; do not describe interface examples as behavior that has already been released.

# Fatal YAML Skip-Tag Troubleshooting Tree

The initial record described a position problem that is difficult to determine from the final result: after a call completes, the caller sees only a few results or none at all, and cannot tell whether the input stopped before processing YAML, or had already entered object processing and then failed to continue because of the tag. The old record pointed both situations to `src/ansiblelint/runner.py`, but that can only be used as the starting point for investigation; the two phenomena must not be treated as having the same cause.

The file header shows `logging`, `multiprocessing`, `multiprocessing.pool`, and `os`. First check whether clues about the input, return, or records were left near runner; parallel-related imports can only suggest that parallel processing may exist nearby, not show that a particular YAML failure has already reached a worker.

```text
Call completed
├─ Load failure information present
│  ├─ No processable object seen → First leave it at the YAML stop point
│  └─ Object already seen       → Investigate object processing next
└─ Processable object already present
   ├─ play has a skip tag       → Record the play-level result
   ├─ task has a skip tag       → Record the task-level result
   └─ Neither has one           → Continue checking normal rule scheduling
```

First save the unmodified input and the first output. An empty final result cannot substitute for load status; failure information cannot substitute for object status. If the input did not form a processable object, do not continue inferring from the rule name or task tag. If the object has formed, inspect play and task separately; do not write one level's tag as if the entire file had been skipped.

The investigation record must include at least four items: whether the input was modified, whether loading succeeded, whether runner received an object, and the raw result after the call. When a rerun is needed, change only one condition in the test input. A failed call and a successful call can be compared only when they use the same type of input; if the inputs differ, save them separately and do not call the difference in results the same kind of short-circuit.

There is currently no concrete sample showing where the two paths converge. When load status or object status cannot be obtained, the stopping position itself is the conclusion; do not use an empty list to fill it in as "not executed" or "already passed."

# Fatal YAML Skip-Tag Troubleshooting Tree

The initial draft treated the two incidents involving "fewer results" together as a runner short circuit. After review, this term is no longer used for branch decisions: Fatal YAML short circuit must be investigated starting with whether the input forms a processable object; Task and play skip-tag dispatch may only be checked after the object already exists. The two may cause callers to see similar final results, but they cannot share recovery actions.

`src/ansiblelint/runner.py` remains the entry point for follow-up checks on this page. The file header shows `logging`, `multiprocessing`, `multiprocessing.pool`, and `os`, so you can first look for records around runner, parallel adjacency, and return locations. Do not treat the YAML failure as a worker failure merely because parallel imports are visible; the current material does not locate any particular failure to a worker.

```text
One lint call
├─ Does the input form a processable object?
│  ├─ No
│  │  ├─ Load-failure output present → Fatal YAML short circuit
│  │  └─ No failure output           → Check the handoff from loader to classification
│  └─ Yes
│     ├─ No dispatch state seen      → Check where the object is handed to runner
│     └─ Already in dispatch         → Check play and task separately
└─ Final result is empty
   └─ Cannot by itself indicate any of the locations above
```

## First lock down the initial incident

Save the original input, the first failure output, the state before the call, and the result after the call. When rerunning after correcting the input, save the corrected output separately; do not overwrite the initial failure incident. Do not first summarize the failure output as a "load error": preserve the distinction between whether it came from the outer call layer or from the loading process layer. If the outer layer does not state whether runner received the input, you cannot use that to jump to the rule-execution branch.

Use short lines when recording:

```text
Input:          original / modified / unconfirmed
Loading:        successful / failed / unconfirmed
Classification: object formed / unconfirmed
runner:         received / not received / unconfirmed
play tag:       original value / none / unconfirmed
task tag:       original value / none / unconfirmed
Before-call result: original content
After-call result:  original content
Stopped at:     loading / classification / object handoff / dispatch / unconfirmed
```

Unconfirmed is not synonymous with blank. It means that no usable record is available here. Filling in unconfirmed as "passed," "not executed," or "rule not matched" causes subsequent investigation to start at a later layer and instead lose the actual stopping point.

## YAML Branch

First ask whether the input was accepted by loader, then whether classification occurred, and only afterward whether runner received the object. If any one step lacks evidence, later rule results cannot be used to infer the preceding step. For example, when there is only a failure message and an empty result, the current wording can be "failure source and object handoff unconfirmed"; it cannot be "the rules did not run," because the empty result may also simply mean that loading did not continue.

Recovery after a loading failure targets the input itself. After preserving the failure sample, a single rerun that changes only the input can confirm the loading status. Repeatedly starting parallel processing does not add evidence about the loading stage; the existence of `multiprocessing` and `multiprocessing.pool` does not change this. If loading succeeds but there are still no results, the next step is to confirm classification and object handoff, not to immediately look for skip tags.

ALR-213 are suitable for saving the visible results of successful and failed calls. When comparing them, first check whether the two calls involve the same class of input, then list the loading status, object status, runner return, and rule results side by side. The specific input has not yet been added to the card, so do not invent a YAML example here, and do not infer from one failure that other YAML forms will all stop in the same way.

## Object and tag branches

Once the object has loaded, Fatal YAML short circuit is no longer the preferred explanation for reduced results. First confirm the object level, then record play and task separately. When a play has `skip_ansible_lint`, the skipped items are the lint rules applicable to that play; this does not directly show that every task under the play is in the same state. When a task has `skip_ansible_lint`, the skipped items are the lint rules applicable to that task; this also does not show what happened with other tasks or during loading.

```text
Object handed to runner
├─ Does play have skip_ansible_lint
│  ├─ Yes → Record the scope of applicable rules at the play level
│  └─ No  → Continue reading task
└─ Does task have skip_ansible_lint
   ├─ Yes → Record the scope of applicable rules at the task level
   └─ No  → Observe normal rule dispatch
```

Do not replace these two levels of records with "the entire playbook was skipped." If you only know that a tag exists, but not whether it is attached to a play or a task, the conclusion stops at the object layer. If you know that a task has a tag but do not know the scope of applicable rules, do not attribute every result absent after the call to the tag; it could also be a rule not being matched, or the call may not have reached that task.

The follow-up check for ALR-230 starts with the state before the call and focuses on whether there were any additional visible changes after completion. During reproduction, keep the object level, the original values of both tags, the before-call result, and the after-call result in the same record. When there are no additional changes after completion, write "No additional changes observed" verbatim; this does not automatically prove that no rules were executed at all.

## Seeing failures and tags at the same time

A failure message, an empty result, and a skip tag can appear near the same input, but the troubleshooting order cannot be reversed. First confirm whether the input loaded successfully; when loading did not succeed, the tag is merely a field in the original and cannot prove that the object entered dispatch. Only after loading succeeds is it worth using the tag to explain changes in object-level results. If the object has formed but runner's receipt status is unclear, check the object handoff first rather than using the tag to fill in the intermediate path.

```text
Failure message + empty result + tag
├─ Loading failed → Preserve the input and failure output; stop at the loading boundary
├─ Loading succeeded, object unconfirmed → Check classification and runner receipt
└─ Object confirmed → Check the play tag and task tag separately
```

## Stopping points

- The original input was modified and can no longer be matched to the first failure output.
- There is only a final empty result, with no loading, classification, or object status.
- The failure message came from the outer layer, and it is still unclear whether runner received the input.
- The tag exists, but its level is unclear.
- The successful and failed calls used different classes of input, yet their short-circuit locations were compared.
- Both play and task have tags, but their rule scopes were not recorded separately.

This page currently retains two gaps: ALR-213 lack a specific input, and ALR-230 have not yet put the scope for a play and task carrying tags simultaneously into the same record. When a new incident becomes available, first fill in the loading, classification, and runner states in the record table, then decide which branch to follow.

# Fatal YAML Skip-Tag Troubleshooting Tree

The earliest incident evidence was sparse: the caller only said that after one lint run, "some results were missing," and the old link pointed to `src/ansiblelint/runner.py`. At the time, there was no original input or object handoff record, only the final list and a vague failure description. The first version therefore put Fatal YAML short circuit and Task and play skip-tag dispatch into the same short-circuit tree. That entry point is still useful because it reminds people not to infer the entire path from the final list; but it is no longer sufficient to determine the cause.

A later review separated the two. The former first asks whether YAML can produce an object that can be processed, while the latter is relevant only after the object already exists and has been handed over to the dispatch process. Both may appear as "no new diagnostics" or "one fewer item than expected," but they sit at different boundaries: one is close to input and loading, and the other is close to the scope of rule applicability at the object layer. If the two are conflated during recovery, the most common outcome is repeatedly rerunning the same call, with the original incident evidence instead overwritten by the corrected input.

`logging`, `multiprocessing`, `multiprocessing.pool`, and `os` are directly visible at the top of the file. These are clues for tracing back through locations adjacent to the runner: records may help confirm whether the input reached the runner, concurrency-related code is worth examining after the object has been formed, and code near operating system calls may affect behavior at the outer layer. They do not establish ownership of the YAML loader, the classification process, or specific rules, nor can they directly pinpoint a particular failure to a worker. Starting the investigation in this file does not mean every step ends in this file.

## First, Pin Down a Single Call in Its Original State

When you encounter "empty results," "one fewer item," or "failure without diagnostics," do not search for rule names first. First collect the input, the first output, and the before-and-after state from the same call. "The same call" matters here: corrected input, output from another entry point, or a later parallel rerun cannot replace the original incident evidence. Keep the original when you can; when you cannot, at least indicate whether the input has already been changed, and do not pass off corrected results as those from the first call.

We recommend recording the incident evidence in a short passage; not every item needs to be known:

```text
Input:             Original / Modified / Not obtained
Loading status:    Succeeded / Failed / Unconfirmed
Content class:     Object formed / Not formed / Unconfirmed
runner received:   Received / Not received / Unconfirmed
Scheduling status: Entered / Not entered / Unconfirmed
play tag:          Original value / None / Unconfirmed
task tag:          Original value / None / Unconfirmed
Result before call: Original content
Result after call:  Original content
Current stopping point: Loading / Classification / Object handoff / Scheduling / Summary / Unconfirmed
```

"Unconfirmed" in the table is not an empty space to be covered up. It means the current evidence does not connect this layer. Do not change unconfirmed to "passed," change it to "not executed," or fill it in as "rule not matched" just because the final list is empty. Each of these three statements requires different preceding states: "passed" requires evidence that processing completed; "not executed" requires confirmation that the object or scheduling did not continue; and "not matched" requires confirmation that rule scheduling occurred.

The first output must remain verbatim next to the call record. If failure information comes from the outer call layer, it can only show that the outer layer saw a failure; it cannot by itself show whether runner received the input. Conversely, if the outer layer did not print a failure, that does not show that YAML loaded successfully. First find the earliest known state among input, loading, classification, and runner receipt, then proceed downward.

```text
Call ended
├─ Did the input form a processable object?
│  ├─ No
│  │  ├─ Loading failure output present → Follow the YAML stop branch
│  │  └─ No failure output     → Check the handoff from loader to classification
│  └─ Yes
│     ├─ runner receipt unknown → Check the object handoff
│     ├─ No scheduling status seen → Check the subsequent status inside runner
│     └─ Scheduling entered     → Examine play and task separately
└─ Only the final result is known to be empty
   └─ Not enough to choose any of the branches above
```

Follow this tree based on visible states, not on guesses about the location from the exception name. Even if descriptions such as "short circuit" or "skip" appear in the incident, first return to the question of whether the object exists. A description may come from the caller's observation; it cannot replace the saved input and state.

## YAML when no object is formed

The investigation of Fatal YAML short circuit starts from the failed output, but does not treat the failed output as the complete conclusion. First confirm whether this output corresponds to the current input; then check whether content classification has already occurred; and then check whether an object that can continue processing has reached the runner. If the input stops before classification, the subsequent rule, play, and task must not be interpreted as normal results of this invocation. If an object or object-level diagnostics already exist, the situation must not be simply documented as a "pure loading failure."

The recovery action for this branch changes only the input. After preserving the failed sample, perform a rerun that changes only the input once to see whether the loading status changes. Do not change the input and labels in the same round and then switch the invocation entry point; even if the output changes, that makes it impossible to determine which layer moved. Preserve the rerun result alongside the first failed output, rather than using the new successful result to overwrite the old failed result.

If the loading phase has already ended, repeatedly starting parallel processing will not produce a loading status. `multiprocessing` and `multiprocessing.pool` only indicate that parallel-processing neighbors exist near the runner file; they cannot automatically move the failure location forward to the worker. When there is no worker-level record, write "worker location not confirmed"; do not designate a nonexistent parallel fault point just to make the tree complete.

Sometimes thecurrentsite only retains failure information and an empty list. First distinguish between two things: whether the failure information was produced by the loading process or by the outer invocation layer; and whether the empty list is part of the returned status or the caller's own aggregation. When neither has been confirmed, stop at the input handoff. Looking at labels or specific rules at this point will only push the judgment into a layer with no evidence.

Even when loading succeeds but the result is still empty, do not immediately jump to "skipped." Continue by asking whether classification completed, whether the runner received an object, and whether dispatch started. If classification is unconfirmed, complete classification first; if object receipt is unconfirmed, complete the handoff first; only when dispatch already has a record but no target result may "there is currently no match" be written as an observation. Empty results at different layers should not share the same explanation.

## ALR-213 Comparison Record

ALR-213 provides a verification entry point where the visible results of both a successful call and a failed call must be retained. When using it, document the two calls separately first, and do not use the successful side as a substitute for the failed side. Comparable fields include whether the inputs are of the same type, which call has a loading-failure output, whether an object was formed, whether the runner returned, whether the results contain rule diagnostics, and whether the caller saw any other changes.

```text
Successful call
  Input category:
  Loading / classification:
  Runner status:
  Returned result:

Failed call
  Input category:
  Loading / classification:
  Runner status:
  Returned result:
```

Compare the differences between the two results only when the input categories and invocation conditions match. If one side uses corrected input and the other uses the original failing input, simply record their respective states; do not declare on that basis that the short-circuit location has been determined.ALR-213 still lack concrete inputs, so do not fabricate a seemingly typical YAML snippet here, or infer the behavior of all YAML forms from a single failure record.

The value of a successful invocation is not to prove that the failed invocation "should have succeeded". It can only help identify which layer's state differed between the two invocations. Nor is the value of a failed invocation to prove that all subsequent rules did not run; its first purpose is to preserve the last state that can be confirmed before execution stopped. When both sides lack classification or runner state, comparing the final diagnostic counts does not provide enough explanatory value.

## Handling after the object already exists

Once YAML has successfully created an object and passed it to the runner, troubleshooting shifts from the input boundary to the object layer. At this point, do not continue using Fatal YAML short circuit to explain changes in results caused by tags. First confirm whether the current object is a play or a task, then read the tags at the corresponding level. play and task are two separate checkpoints; a single "skipped" description cannot replace both checkpoints.

When a play has `skip_ansible_lint`, execution of the lint rules applicable to that play is skipped. When recording this, first preserve whether the play was recognized, the original tag value, and the known scope of the rules. Do not extend this conclusion to "the entire file failed to load", or automatically record every task under the play as having the same state. YAML being loadable, the play being skipped, and a particular task producing no diagnostics are observations at different levels.

```text
The object has entered the runner
├─ Does the play have skip_ansible_lint
│  ├─ Yes → Record the scope of applicable rules at the play level
│  └─ No → Continue reading the task
└─ Does the task have skip_ansible_lint
   ├─ Yes → Record the scope of applicable rules at the task level
   └─ No → Continue observing normal rule scheduling
```

When a task has `skip_ansible_lint`, what is skipped is the execution of lint rules applicable to that task. It is not YAML loading failure, nor is it the execution record of another task. Only if the task does not have this label should you continue by checking ordinary rule scheduling and the results of specific rules. When there is no new content after the call, at least three possibilities have not been ruled out: the task was skipped, the rule already ran but did not match anything, or the call never reached this task. Without the object and scheduling state, do not arbitrarily write any one of these as the conclusion.

Records at the play level can remain very brief:

```text
Was play recognized:  Yes / No / Unconfirmed
play raw label:      Original value
Rule scope:          Known / Unconfirmed
Result before call:  Original content
Result after call:   Original content
```

The task level should also have its own line of record, rather than copying from the play line:

```text
Did task get reached: Original value
 task raw label:      Original value
Rule scope:           Known / Unconfirmed
Result before call:   Original content
Result after call:    Original content
```

When the label field was not read correctly, stop at object parsing or object handoff. Do not use another task's result to replace the current play's label status, and do not assume that all reduced diagnostics were caused by a play merely because that play has a label. When one result item is missing, you also need to know at which object level that item should have appeared before you can begin checking the label at the corresponding level.

## Labels appear on both play and task

Labels appearing at both levels are the situation most easily obscured by the statement "the entire playbook was skipped." During handling, first preserve both original values, then record the applicable scope for each separately. Do not assume that the task label inherits the play's determination, and do not assert that one level overrides the other without records. The current material does not provide the complete scope when labels appear at both levels, so this page only requires that the levels be kept separate in the record.

```text
Two labels seen in the same call
├─ play label: Preserve the original value and confirm the play-level scope
├─ task label: Preserve the original value and confirm the task-level scope
├─ Fewer results: Confirm which object level the missing item belongs to
└─ Incomplete scope: Stop at scope confirmation; do not write an override relationship
```

If you obtained only the label text without the object level, first confirm where the label is attached. If the object level is clear and the label is also clear, but the applicable rule scope was not obtained, recording "scope unconfirmed" is sufficient. Turning an unknown scope into a global skip would erase the distinction between play and task and would also explain away rule results that could still have been observed.

The trace-back for ALR-230 starts with the pre-call state, focusing on whether any additional visible changes were left behind after processing. When using it for this branch, keep the object hierarchy, play tag, task tag, pre-call result, and post-call result together. If there are no additional changes after completion, leave this observation as-is; it does not by itself prove that no rules were executed, and it certainly cannot show that the scopes of the two levels are the same.

## When Failure Messages and Tags Coexist

Near the same input, there may be a failure message, an empty result, and a skip tag at the same time. The most dangerous approach is to assign cause directly based on the message text. First rule out the possibilities in order: whether the input loaded successfully; whether the object was formed; whether the runner received it; whether the object entered scheduling; and only then examine play and task separately.

```text
Failure message + empty result + skip tag
├─ Loading failed
│  └─ Preserve the fixed input and failure output; the tag cannot prove that scheduling was reached
├─ Loading succeeded, object unconfirmed
│  └─ Trace back the classification and runner receipt
├─ Object confirmed, scheduling unconfirmed
│  └─ Trace back the state after the object handoff
└─ Scheduling reached
   └─ Check the tag scopes of play and task separately
```

Failure messages and tags can each explain only a local aspect. A loading failure belongs to the input boundary; a tag skip belongs to the object-scheduling boundary. Both situations may occur under different conditions in the same workflow, but the latter cannot explain the former. If the failure occurs during loading, the tag may simply be part of the original text, so it cannot be used to show that the object entered rule processing. If loading has succeeded, the tag becomes evidence for explaining changes in the object-level result.

When the caller says, "There is a tag, so there is no error," first ask which object the tag belongs to, which result item it refers to, and whether loading and scheduling states are available. If these states are missing, record the statement as an on-site description, not a final determination. Conversely, when a loading failure is seen, do not delete the tag from the input and then claim that recovery has already occurred; first have the input-loading layer confirmed independently.

## Perform Recovery Actions by Layer

Recovery is not a matter of repeating the same call. First preserve the original state, then change only one known condition in the current branch. When loading fails, the thing to modify is the test input; when the object has loaded but the tag scope is unclear, the thing to modify is the tag record or the object-level observation; only after ordinary rule scheduling has been confirmed should you investigate the rule itself. If a rerun changes the input, tags, and entry point at the same time, the output change can no longer be explained.

The recommended order of operations is as follows:

1. Freeze the original input artifact and the first output to prevent the failed sample from being overwritten by a corrected file.
2. Clearly state whether the loader returned a failure, an object, or has not yet been confirmed; do not use an empty list in place of this item.
3. When there is an object, continue confirming its classification and whether runner received it.
4. Read the original labels for play and task separately only when scheduling is already visible.
5. Compare the diagnostics before and after the call only after the rule scope is clear.
6. Compare the status differences between successful and failed calls only when they use the same type of input.
7. If it still cannot be explained after reaching the last known state, stop at that layer and retain the gap in the record.

This sequence is not intended to turn every incident into a complete table. Its purpose is to prevent cross-layer recovery: using changed labels to handle a loading failure, or using rerun input to explain an already-confirmed task skip, will both expand the unknowns. Stop at loading when loading can be confirmed, and stop at the object when the object can be confirmed; subsequent steps are triggered by newly added state, not by "the result looks wrong."

## Scope of runner file usage

`src/ansiblelint/runner.py` can serve as an entry point for viewing runner's adjacent state: when looking for locations adjacent to the input, object, return, and record, start here. `logging` may help locate the vicinity of retained records, while `multiprocessing` and `multiprocessing.pool` remind investigators to pay attention to parallel adjacency; `os` indicates that the file also contains operating-system-related calls. Up to this point, these are only local clues supported by the file header and the old entry point.

Do not write this path as YAML, with the loader, content classification, rule execution, and final aggregation all confirmed to occur in the same place. Nor should you skip the actual input and object states just because the old investigation started from runner. When further tracing back is necessary, record "which layer of state to continue looking for from runner adjacency," rather than filling in a complete implementation ownership for the incident.

## Common stopping points

**The input has been modified.** When it cannot be matched to the first failed output, stop comparing the short-circuit positions before and after the modification. Retain the currently known state and wait for the original sample or an equivalent record.

**Only the final empty list is available.** When the empty list contains no loading, classification, object handoff, or scheduling information, stop at the call-result layer. Do not write that all checks passed, and do not write that the skip already occurred.

**The failure comes from the outer call layer.** An outer-layer failure cannot show that runner received the input. First check whether the input arrived and whether an object was formed; do not switch directly to the rule or labels.

**Only the presence of a skip tag is known.** If it is unknown whether the tag is attached to a play or a task, do not draw a conclusion about its scope. First confirm the object level and the original tag location.

**A task is known to have been skipped, but the scope is unknown.** Keep the observation at the task level; do not attribute all missing results to that tag.

**The play has a tag, but task results are used as proof.** Evidence from the two levels is not interchangeable. Record each level's objects, tags, and results separately.

**Trying to confirm a loading failure through parallel reruns.** Without new loading or object state information, reruns will only produce more results; they will not identify the stopping point.

**Success and failure used different inputs.** Record the two calls separately; do not use them as a direct comparison of short-circuit behavior.

**There are fewer results, but no pre-call state is available.** Only post-call observations can be described; it is not possible to determine whether the reduction occurred during dispatch or aggregation.

## Retained old statement and current starting points

The statement in the early notes that "both failure and skipping cause the runner to return immediately" is retained here because it explains why the old records started investigating from the runner. It is no longer the current assessment: Fatal YAML short circuit goes back to the loading boundary; Task and play skip-tag dispatch goes back to the object dispatch boundary. Both may change the results seen by the caller, but that does not mean they should share input recovery, tag evaluation, or rule scope.

The interim review filled in the layered approach, but did not fill in the specific samples. ALR-213 is still used to check the comparative states of successful and failed calls; ALR-230 is still used to confirm the object level from the pre-call state and any additional changes after the call. The two cards only provide starting points for verification; they do not replace the branch records on this page. The currently unconfirmed items also remain unchanged: the specific input for Fatal YAML short circuit has not been added; the complete before-and-after states of successful and failed calls have not yet been aligned; the actual rule scope when both play and task have tags has not appeared in a single incident record; the local relationship between the runner and object classification cannot be determined solely from the file header.

When the next incident record is obtained, first fill in the input, loading, classification, and runner states. Read the play and task tags only if these states establish that the stopping point has reached object dispatch. Without new state information, do not extend the assessment to later stages.

# Task Naming Compatibility Migration Guide

First separate task-name checks from the single "unnamed task" issue. The current troubleshooting entry point is `test/rules/test_unnamed_task.py`; the file also introduces `RulesCollection`, `TaskHasNameRule`, and `Runner`. Taken together, these three objects indicate at minimum that this does not only check the rule class itself; it also passes through the rule collection and the runtime entry point.

The old configuration still contains `unnamed-task`. During migration, do not first conflate it with the case-sensitivity issue into a single switch: missing names and first-letter capitalization are two separate boundaries. The former should continue to be confirmed based on whether the task has a name; the latter should only be rechecked once a name already exists.

Proposed approach:

1. First collect the configurations and inline comments that still contain `unnamed-task`.
2. Use the test entry point to confirm whether the rule is included in the collection, then check the matches produced by Runner.
3. Keep a separate set of case-variation samples; do not substitute missing-name samples.

# Task Naming Compatibility Migration Notes

After this review, the migration still starts with `test/rules/test_unnamed_task.py`, but the filename can no longer be treated as a complete description of the rule's semantics. The file directly shows:

```python
from ansiblelint.rules import RulesCollection
from ansiblelint.rules.unnamed_task import TaskHasNameRule
from ansiblelint.runner import Runner
```

The investigation order is therefore now to check whether `TaskHasNameRule` enters `RulesCollection`, then use the result from `Runner` to determine whether the rule did not run or ran and produced a diagnostic different from what was expected. Attributing every discrepancy to the legacy-label migration, as we did before, was too broad.

## Legacy Entry Cleanup

Historical configuration and comments may still use `unnamed-task`. For compatibility, it should be interpreted as `name[missing]`, rather than left as a separate rule name. The impact is small: existing ignore entries still describe "task has no name," while the current label shown to callers is consistently `name[missing]`.

The migration checklist should be kept in two columns; it cannot be completed in one pass by replacing strings:

| Location of the legacy form | Result to check during migration |
| --- | --- |
| Rule configuration | Whether `unnamed-task` is interpreted as `name[missing]` |
| Suppression comment on the task line | Whether it skips only the missing-name check |
| Regression samples | Whether unnamed tasks still reach the naming rule |

"Interpreted as" does not mean every repository must change the literal immediately. Existing configuration can keep the legacy label; new samples and newly written documentation should prefer `name[missing]`. If someone changes the configuration first and then finds that Runner returns no results, they will not be able to distinguish a compatibility-mapping problem from the rule never having been collected.

## Keep Casing Checks Separate

When a name exists but starts with a lowercase letter, the diagnostic label is `name[casing]`. It and `name[missing]` should not use the same sample, nor should they share the migration assessment for "ignore unnamed tasks." When a task has no `name`, there is no text to check for casing; when a task has a name but its first letter does not meet the requirement, the legacy unnamed-task label cannot be used to suppress that result either.

An older note said, "Adding any name is enough to pass the naming check." That statement is suitable only for a temporary manual check, not as a migration conclusion. The added name may still trigger `name[casing]`, so the review needs two steps: first have the missing-name sample produce `name[missing]`, then separately have the lowercase-name sample produce `name[casing]`.

```
Old handling
  unnamed-task ──> treated as the entire naming issue

Handling after separation
  unnamed-task ──> name[missing]
  Existing but lowercase name ──> name[casing]
```

## Fallback Retained for Now

If a caller's legacy configuration produces unexpected matches after migration, first restore the original `unnamed-task` form. Do not change the name text, suppression comments, and rule set at the same time. After restoring it, inspect the same three objects through the same test entry point: `TaskHasNameRule`, `RulesCollection`, and `Runner`. This at least preserves the distinction between "legacy-label interpretation failed" and "the rule's execution scope changed."

This page currently covers only the boundaries around missing task names and the first letter of task names. Naming issues for play or import are recorded elsewhere; the same migration steps cannot be inferred from the task samples here.
versions.change_summary: Separate legacy-label review from casing review
