# Task Naming Compatibility Migration Notes

This record is still often opened as the "operating instructions after the naming rules were changed," but it was originally just a migration note focused on missing task names. The retained old steps are useful: they explain why some configurations still contain `unnamed-task`, and they can indicate where to start troubleshooting. However, the old steps treated naming issues too simplistically; that position was later revised during review.

Keep the original entry point for now. `test/rules/test_unnamed_task.py` was the verification point left at the time. At the top of the file, the three objects are placed together:

```python
from ansiblelint.rules import RulesCollection
from ansiblelint.rules.unnamed_task import TaskHasNameRule
from ansiblelint.runner import Runner
```

This reference is enough to limit this page to a narrow scope: the relationship between the rule type, rule collection, and execution entry point. It does not describe the call history of all name checks, and it should not be used to infer the behavior of plays, imports, or other rules. When someone later searches by filename for the "unnamed task" logic, start here to distinguish whether the rule was not added to the collection, the Runner did not execute, or the label in the execution result was not as expected.

## Early Migration Approach (Retained)

The earliest approach was straightforward: find `unnamed-task` in the configuration and treat them as the old form of the unnamed-task check; run the rule with a task sample that has no name; and consider the migration complete when it produced a match. At the time, "adding a name to the task" was also written up as a quick recovery measure.

This approach solved one localized problem: old configurations did not have to fail immediately because a label had been renamed. The compatibility relationship should still be retained as `unnamed-task` explaining `name[missing]`. Existing configurations and old inline suppressions can continue to express the original intent; newly written configurations, samples, and documentation should use `name[missing]` directly.

The problem with the early steps was not the old label itself, but that they merged all name-related results into a single check. After a task changed from "no name" to "having a name," the check did not naturally end. The first letter of the name could still produce another result, and the old record did not document this boundary.

> Old conclusion: Once any name is added, the naming rule no longer needs to be reviewed.
>
> This conclusion no longer applies. It can only indicate that the missing-name branch may have been cleared; it does not indicate that the name text satisfies other requirements.

## Two Tracks to Retain During Migration

Missing names and casing must be handled with two samples and two expected outcomes. A task without `name` should produce `name[missing]`; a task with an existing name whose first letter is lowercase should produce `name[casing]`. The latter is neither an additional label for the former nor a substitute for the former's result.

The migration table does not need to become a global label table. It only needs to place the current caller's old entry in the corresponding branch:

| Situation | What to check first | Post-migration determination |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The configuration still uses `unnamed-task` | Whether the compatibility mapping is active | It should map to `name[missing]` |
| The task does not have `name` | Whether the rule enters `RulesCollection` | The Runner result should retain the missing-name diagnosis |
| The task has a name, but it starts with a lowercase letter | The name text itself | The result should be `name[casing]` |
| The name and old label were changed at the same time | Revert one of the changes first | Do not determine two migration actions from one result |

The third row was added later. The old sample covered only "no name," while the casing check depends on an already existing name text. Changing the same task into different forms one after another for verification makes the results appear consistent, but actually loses the source of the failure. Two independent samples make it easier to see whether a change affected compatibility mapping, rule collection, or name evaluation.

The notation ASCII is as follows, for those still troubleshooting with the old configuration:

```text
Legacy config or old comment
    |
    +-- unnamed-task
    |       |
    |       +-- Compatibility interpretation
    |               |
    |               +-- name[missing]
    |
Existing task name
    |
    +-- Starts with a lowercase letter
            |
            +-- name[casing]
```

The two branches in the diagram do not converge. Do not force the second branch back into the old label just to make the report "contain only one naming issue." Doing so mixes the compatibility intent in the configuration with the intent of checking the name text; afterward, even if only one suppression is changed, it is difficult to tell which type of task was affected.

## Handling Old Inline Suppressions

The old notes documented only configuration migration and omitted suppressions on task lines. When the inline form `# noqa:` is followed by a rule label, it records an exact line-level skip. When migrating this type of comment, do not generalize it into "skip all name checks." If the old comment uses `unnamed-task`, it still expresses the missing-name branch; the casing result should be evaluated separately.

This also changes the rollback order. Previously, the recommendation was to restore the old label, restore the task name, and delete the comment all at once as soon as the result looked abnormal. That would erase the most valuable distinctions. The order now retained is:

1. First restore the label in the configuration or comment and confirm whether the old compatibility entry point can still be interpreted.
2. Do not change the task name; confirm whether `TaskHasNameRule` is collected in `RulesCollection`.
3. Still do not change the sample form; only check whether the result produced by `Runner` is a missing name, a casing issue, or no match.
4. Only after the first three steps are stable should you modify the name text separately and review `name[casing]`.

What this restores is not "one master switch," but one specific migration action. The first step is especially important for callers that still depend on the old label; if the old label is changed to the new label immediately, the result change cannot show whether the compatibility mapping was involved.

## The Merged Approach That Was Once Used and Later Abandoned

There was once a simplified approach: put missing names, initial-letter casing, and all old-label replacements into one regression test case, expecting a single Runner output to show that the naming-rule migration was complete. It appeared to save samples, but had two practical drawbacks.

First, a task with a missing name has no name text and cannot also serve as a casing counterexample. To make one test case cover both situations, the test would change the input form midway, so the final output would no longer correspond to one stable object. Second, the compatibility interpretation of the old label occurs at the configuration or suppression entry point, while casing is evaluated on the content of an existing name; tying the two together causes "no match" to be misread as a problem on either side.

Therefore, this merged approach was not retained as a migration step. It is still included here because the test expectations in some old branches may be arranged according to this approach. When you encounter such an arrangement, do not conclude from it that the runtime has only one naming diagnosis; split the samples first, then see what each sample actually leaves behind after passing through the Runner.

## Current Review Entry Point

A recent review of name validation still has one unconfirmed item. The related navigation is at ALR-214. The blocker on the card is that the required old-version image has been cleaned up, so that image can no longer be used to replay the early scenario. This limitation corrects the stronger wording used earlier on this page: the fact that the current path can still be opened does not mean that every combination of the old configuration has been reproduced.

The only objects that can still be checked are the three locations near the current entry point:

- `TaskHasNameRule`: Confirm whether the naming-rule object is still visible on the current path.
- `RulesCollection`: Confirm whether the rule was included in the collection when the issue occurred.
- `Runner`: Confirm that the label was not conflated in the middle after the result came out of the execution entry point.

These three locations are not a complete substitute for the historical record. They are simply the verification path that can still be retained today. When the old image is unavailable, do not fabricate a conclusion that the "old environment has been verified," and do not backfill the current run result as evidence that the early migration succeeded.

## Correction to the Old Assessment

The old version described `test/rules/test_unnamed_task.py` as the "final verification of the compatibility mapping." This statement needs to be narrowed. That path is suitable for locating adjacent objects in task-name-related tests, but it cannot by itself prove that every old configuration, every inline suppression, or every type of Runner invocation went through the same mapping.

The more accurate way to use it is: when a caller reports a behavior change in the old label, first save the original configuration and task text; then observe the missing-name sample and lowercase-name sample separately; only afterward decide whether the configuration needs to be changed. If the issue occurs only with the old label, prioritize checking the interpretation from `unnamed-task` through `name[missing]`. If the issue occurs only with an existing lowercase name, check `name[casing]` directly; do not migrate the old label first.

Name-related scenarios outside task names should not be extrapolated from here. The naming records for play and import are in DOC-24; they share the search term "naming rules" with this page, but the sample objects are different. This page does not contain enough material to provide a migration order for them.

## Old Operating Note Still Retained at the End of the Page

The following section was once used for quick troubleshooting and is retained for people who need to understand the old reports:

```text
See a naming issue
  -> Add a name first
  -> Run again
  -> If there is no result, stop
```

This section should not be executed directly now. It ignores compatibility with the old label and also ignores the casing result that may appear after adding a name. It is retained not as a recommendation, but to explain why some old records only say "passed after adding a name."

The only part that can safely be carried forward now is the separation principle: handle old aliases under the missing-name branch; handle existing names under the text rules; do not treat one result as proof that both types of boundary have been verified. Until the image is restored, the unconfirmed area indicated by ALR-214 should remain unconfirmed.

Prefixes derived for task files will initially be recorded as a naming-rule issue, rather than tracked separately as Runner behavior. The existing entry point is `test/rules/test_unnamed_task.py`; filenames can easily steer the discussion toward "unnamed tasks," but what needs to be retained here is the prefix relationship between the task name and the task file.

The only adjacent objects reviewed so far are `RulesCollection`, `TaskHasNameRule`, and `Runner`. They show that the test passes through the rule set, the naming-rule object, and the execution entry point, but they are not enough to show which of these objects generates the prefix.

Two handling constraints for now:

- Record prefix issues separately from tasks that lack a name. The former has at least a name to compare; the latter does not.
- Future regression will still start from this test file; once the actual assertion is visible, decide whether to change the rule implementation or the caller side.

versions.body:
# Task File Prefix Decision Record

The prefix derived from the task file remains covered by the name-rule contract. This review did not turn it into input shaping in the Runner, nor did it merge it into the "task has no name" branch. The scope of the decision is narrow: regression clues for the prefix check remain near the name-rule tests; the rule, collection, and execution entry are each handled only according to their confirmed adjacency relationships.

When this page was first created, the only entry point was `test/rules/test_unnamed_task.py`. This path introduced a very practical misreading: unnamed in the filename makes it easy to collapse every name-related failure into a missing task name. Doing so saves one distinction, but loses the input state of the failure. A task with no name has no text to compare; a task with an existing name that does not satisfy the prefix derived from the file has a different comparison condition. The same rule object may encounter both cases, but that does not mean they should appear with the same problem description, the same sample, or the same reason for remediation.

The draft did not find a caller that still used this prefix at the time, so it did not include any fixed prefix text, nor did it assume where the filename stem would be obtained. This gap remains. Adding an unverified file example, template format, or error message would make later readers think it was existing behavior rather than a condition that still needs to be identified from the caller and test assertions.

## Objects Confirmed During Review

The direct imports visible in the test file are:

```python
from ansiblelint.rules import RulesCollection
from ansiblelint.rules.unnamed_task import TaskHasNameRule
from ansiblelint.runner import Runner
```

These three items are enough to establish that this is not an isolated test that only checks a string: the rule object needs to enter the rule collection, and the execution entry is also within the test's adjacency scope. They cannot by themselves answer "who generates the prefix." The class name of `TaskHasNameRule` only indicates that the name rule is the first object to inspect; `RulesCollection` indicates that the rule is organized into a collection; `Runner` indicates that an execution entry exists. Interpreting import order as responsibility ownership, especially writing `Runner` directly as the prefix source, would expand the current material into an implementation conclusion that has not appeared.

This review did not rewrite the conservative separation in the draft; it only turned it from a temporary notation into an explicit decision: file source, task name, and rule execution are three types of information that must be examined separately. The file source determines whether a prefix is expected; the task name determines whether there is an object to compare; the execution entry helps explain why a result appeared or did not appear only after the first two have been established.

## Three Classifications Considered

The first approach was to treat the prefix derived from the file as a subdivision of unnamed tasks. Its advantage is that the entry path already exists and the related tests are also concentrated there. The problem is that it would write "no `name`" and "`name` exists but does not have the expected prefix" as the same type of failure. The former cannot perform a name comparison, while the latter is a failed comparison; if the same record is written only as unnamed, it is impossible to tell whether the caller omitted a field or passed an unexpected name. This approach is not adopted.

The second approach was to treat the prefix as text added by `Runner` before execution. Under this interpretation, investigation would first trace the execution entry, task collection, and result return. The current material does not show that `Runner` holds prefix configuration, rewrites the task name, or is responsible for extracting a name fragment from the task file. The test file's import of `Runner` indicates execution adjacency, not evidence that it gives the prefix meaning. This approach is not adopted; it will be reconsidered only when an assertion, call site, or explicit input-rewriting fragment appears.

The third approach was to treat it as an independent check condition under the name rule. This approach preserves two things: the task must already have a name, and that name must also satisfy the prefix expectation established by the task file. It does not require creating a new rule ID, nor does it require specifying in advance that the check must be located in a particular method of `TaskHasNameRule`; what is decided here is the classification and review order, not the implementation location. This approach is adopted.

"Independent check condition" does not mean an independent execution stage. Rule objects may share preparation work, configuration reads, or a result channel, but the prefix condition cannot be replaced by a missing name. If a sample has neither a task name nor sufficient file-source information, seeing the first name-related result still does not show whether the prefix condition was actually computed. Such a sample may remain in the regression set, but it is not suitable as the sole basis for this prefix behavior.

## Decision Made

The decision on this page is: regress the task-file-derived prefix as a name-rule issue, with `TaskHasNameRule` as the first object to inspect and `test/rules/test_unnamed_task.py` retained as the regression entry. `RulesCollection` and `Runner` are recorded as objects within the same test-adjacency scope; this does not establish that they have prefix semantics.

This decision changes the investigation order. First confirm whether the test construction contains both a task source and a task name; then confirm the name value seen by the name rule; only then examine whether the rule collection and execution entry affect result collection. If the first two items have not been established, even a normally completed execution cannot show that the file-derived prefix was compared. Once the first two items have been established, it is worth tracing whether the result was filtered by the collection, replaced during execution, or never entered this rule at all.

Modification suggestions should also be assessed in this order. Only when the task name is missing should the missing-name state be handled first; it should not be disguised as a prefix mismatch. When the name exists but the prefix does not match, the record should preserve the relationship between the task file and the name; the test filename must not replace the actual input. If later samples show that the two checks share configuration or result forms, a compatibility note can be added; until then, shared behavior must not be inferred from a shared class name.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> TestEntry
    TestEntry: test/rules/test_unnamed_task.py
    TestEntry --> RuleObject
    RuleObject: TaskHasNameRule
    RuleObject --> RuleCollection
    RuleCollection: RulesCollection
    RuleCollection --> RuntimeEntry
    RuntimeEntry: Runner
```

The diagram shows the inspection order decided on this page, not the call direction among these objects. The test file, name rule, rule collection, and execution entry are all present in the known material; the arrows are only intended to prevent reviewers from first guessing from the execution object in place of the name condition.

## Handling Failures in Legacy Calls

ALR-216 is the navigation entry for this record. The observation retained on the card is "File-derived task prefixes legacy-call failure," and it explicitly requires finding the caller that still uses this behavior and checking the actual version, entry point, and current result. This to-do was not automatically completed because the branch entered review.

The subsequent actions on the card show that the issue underwent a capacity review and then moved from To Do to In Review; the reason at the time was that the existing branch was complete and moved directly to review. Here, "branch complete" is not written as meaning that the prefix path has been fully restored. It only indicates that handling continued from the initial capacity check into review. Whether the caller still uses the old entry, whether it passes a task file or an already-processed name, and whether the current result covers prefix comparison still need to be supplied by the actual call side.

Therefore, when the caller reports a call to `Runner`, first treat it as an execution clue. If the report contains only a task-file path, with no task mapping or name value, it can only show that the file may have participated in the input; it cannot confirm that prefix comparison occurred. Conversely, if the report contains only a name string with no file source, it is likewise impossible to determine why that name should have a particular prefix. Both must appear together to constitute the minimum input relationship required by this issue.

This handling will make the early records look less polished: some legacy failures can only be labeled "execution reachable," not "prefix condition verified." Preserving this distinction is more useful than filling in attribution prematurely. It prevents later people from repeatedly tracing the execution entry for the same error while overlooking the correspondence between task source and name that has not yet been established.

## Boundaries of Regression Samples

When adding samples later, at least two states should be distinguished. The first state is that the task has no name; it is used to confirm that a missing name is not mistakenly written as a prefix failure. The second state is that the task name exists but does not match the expectation derived from the task file; it is used to confirm that the prefix condition is not obscured by the first state. The two do not need to be implemented in the same sample, and the test-file path should not be used to replace the input value.

If a sample omits both the name and the file source, its result cannot be used to determine whether the decision on this page took effect. If a sample has a name but no identifiable task source, it may continue to be used for other name-rule checks, but it cannot take responsibility for regression of the file-derived prefix. If a sample has both a task source and a name but only goes through collection construction without entering the execution entry, it may still help locate the comparison on the rule side, but it cannot be used to determine result collection during full execution. These distinctions are not intended to establish a fixed test matrix for every combination; they are intended to prevent different problems from being put back into the same "name failure" when new cases are added.

The current material does not provide a specific filename, specific template text, assertion output, or configuration key. This page does not specify whether the prefix is the full filename, the stem, a directory fragment, or another form, nor does it specify the priority of multiple templates. What may be added must be an actual relationship visible in the caller or assertions; until then, the classification decision remains "file-derived prefix condition under the name rule."

## Separate Handling from the Terminal Name Template

DOC-26 records the interface review for the terminal name template. Both pages involve name text, but the objects differ: this page is concerned with how the task file participates in judging the task-name prefix, while that page is concerned with the terminal name template. The fact that both issues contain "name" or "template" does not justify combining them into the same rule modification.

Only when the same caller both provides the task-file source and uses the terminal name template is it necessary to record their order on the call side. Even then, the caller's actual version and entry point should be confirmed first, rather than inferring a shared implementation from the adjacent topics of the two documents. DOC-26 is not a substitute basis for this page's prefix conclusion; this page likewise does not decide the semantics of the terminal template on its behalf.

## Notes for Next Update

The next update should add only material directly related to the current decision: the entry point and version of a caller that still uses this prefix; the actual combinations of task source and name value in tests; and information showing whether the prefix check is located in the name-rule object or in a fragment within the execution adjacency. Associate new failure phenomena with ALR-216 first, then determine whether they change the classification here.

Until this material appears, maintain three conclusions: the file-derived prefix is regressed from the name-rule entry point; an unnamed task is not its substitute description; `Runner` is not the default ownership.

# Signal Dashboard Cache Trade-off Decision Record

In the regression materials for `ansiblelint-quality-signal`, the debate centered on two options: continue using the existing `regression evidence` records, or split out `Lintable`. The two paths have different failure exits. Combining them would make the failure samples from test and spec look like the same kind of signal.

The approaches compared at the time were:

- Rebuild the environment, then collect results from a clean entry point. This would appear easier to verify, but would replace the state already captured under the current revision; the cache, entry point, and failure samples from that time could no longer serve as a single comparison set.
- Keep the current revision and run a single-variable comparison in the original environment. The cost is that the old entry point and cache would still introduce noise; one rerun cannot be treated as evidence that the environment has recovered.
- Split out `Lintable`. This would allow content recognition and quality signals to be handled separately, but at the time there were no active callers of `Jinja expression`, and it had not been decided whether a rollback should only restore the old entry point.

The decision was to keep the current revision first, without rebuilding the environment. `ansiblelint-quality-signal` would remain the reference state for comparison. Keep the current entry point and command fixed when comparing, and replace only the revision; do not change the environment, cache, and recording method together in a single result. This decision preserves the comparison conditions from that time. It does not mean that cached results already represent the latest state, or that the two failure exits have been merged.

Splitting `Lintable` remains only a supporting direction, because its failure exit differs from that of `regression evidence`. Areas without materials from active callers are not settled by this decision. In particular, who should receive `Jinja expression` and whether rollback restores the old entry point remain open; recording them as completed would change the point in time represented by this record.

Field notes appended to the original record: the objection was that keeping the old environment would continue to carry cache issues into the Quality Signal Dashboard. The later exit actions did not bring the rollback states into alignment either; when the window closed, the current entry point still showed the old value. "Keep" here therefore applies only to the current revision needed for comparison, and does not mean that the exit actions were completed. The original materials remain in `docs/adj-ansiblelint/decisions/ansiblelint-quality-signal-cache and original state trade-offs.md`. Any later change to the decision should be added as a new version.

# Caller Entry-Point Migration Index

The migration records for `copying-client-integration` remain centralized in `docs/adj-copying/migration/current-entry-old-entry-migration-index.md`. This index does not count usage based on how many times something appears in a directory; instead, it keeps the old entry point, replacement location, input version, and recheck records for a real call sample together. When a caller enters through the old name, it should still be possible to find it along the original record; even if the replacement location has been renamed, that must not be used to rewrite the failure state from that time.

This page lists only the real call samples, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback formed by example. Each sample has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit conditions. Notes that cannot be traced back through the index remain expired; do not replace them with similar directories, entry-point names added later, or successful output from elsewhere. In particular, a caller that is still unconfirmed must not be removed from the old path just because another user has completed migration.

The earliest documented tradeoff was whether to continue along `rule profile` or split `YAML loader` into a separate entry point. At the time, the failure exits of the two call paths were different, the actual users of `rule authoring` had not been confirmed, and it was likewise undecided whether reverting should restore only the old entry point. This decision remains in the index's historical section: it shows that the two lines were not merged at the time; it is not a unified naming rule for later batches.

Later trial records wrote `Ansible content` as the location to compare and retained `rule profile` as the trial line. All three names may appear in the surrounding materials for the same call, but they have different meanings: `YAML loader` is the split entry point discussed earlier, `rule profile` is the destination used by the trial line at that time, and `Ansible content` is the replacement location that the index continues to track. When checking the records, first identify the entry point the caller actually used, then see where it was sent this time; do not collapse them into one object based only on search hits.

```text
Caller still in use
        │
        ├── Old entry point ──> Original input ──> First result
        │                         │
        │                         └── Input version and caller version
        │
        └── Replacement location ──> New result ──> Second call
                                      │
                                      ├── Consistent: retain confirmation for this batch
                                      └── Inconsistent: return to old entry point for recheck
```

## Scope of a Single Index Record

An index row is not just "switched" or "not switched." The old-entry-point column retains the location it originally pointed to, the version still used by the caller, and the first result before migration. The replacement-location column records the name actually entered during this trial; do not prematurely write a planned name as the current entry point. The caller column records only objects that have been found and confirmed; if something was inferred only from a directory, report title, or similarly named path, it remains in the pending-verification area.

The batch column records what changed in this batch only. For entry-point migration, the most useful boundary is one caller, one input, and one entry-point change. If both the entry-point name and call parameters change, or a side-channel call is brought in at the same time, the result cannot show which change caused it even if it looks normal. Such a record should be split: first retain the comparison between the old entry point and the replacement location, then record the parameter or side-channel change in the next batch.

The recovery column should not say only "can be rolled back." It needs to record which old entry point the new location was rolled back to, which input was used for the recheck, and what result was obtained after recovery. The purpose of a recovery record is to preserve the comparison baseline. It must not erase an error from the new entry point or rewrite a failed sample as a successful samplewholereasoned later.

It is recommended to fill in a row in the following order, rather than changing the entry point first and adding the materials afterward:

1. Find the caller still in use and note the old entry-point name in the index.
2. Retain the original input and the version currently used by the caller; if the first result contains an error, retain the error as-is.
3. Specify the replacement location for this batch. Migrate only this caller; do not also change a same-named side channel.
4. Record the result from the new entry point and the status of one second call.
5. If the results differ or cannot be explained, return to the old entry point, recheck using the input retained before migration, and write the recovery location back into this batch.

This order serves the current index only. It does not require all callers to migrate at the same time, nor does it use the new entry point appearing in the directory as a prerequisite to begin. For an object that does not yet have the original input, leaving it pending verification is more useful than filling in an apparently complete "migrated" status.

## Constraints Carried Over from Earlier Batches

Earlier records compared the two entry-point lines side by side because their failure exits were different. When using the index later, this earlier decision should not be understood to mean that "all entry points must be migrated independently"; it only reminds maintainers not to treat two unverified call segments as the same path. If the current batch can clearly identify the old entry point, replacement location, and caller, it can proceed independently; when they cannot be identified, continue to retain the unconfirmed status from the earlier section.

The relationship between `rule profile` and `Ansible content` must also be read by batch. A trial may first go through `rule profile`, while the index's replacement location subsequently points to `Ansible content`. This is not an automatic redirect. A caller may mark the corresponding old path as migrated only after its own input and results have been recorded. Even if another caller uses the same name, its input, version, and result must be recorded again.

How long the old entry point remains readable is determined by the callers still using it, not by whether a particular trial batch passes. An object that has already migrated may stop maintaining its own old path; the old name must still remain in the index so historical queries can return to the original record. For other objects that have not yet been confirmed, the recovery entry point and batch status remain valid.

## Two Results During a Trial

The first result answers: what did this original input produce when it came from the replacement location? It may be a success, an error, or a difference that has not yet been categorized. The second call is not used to produce a better-looking result; it is used to confirm whether the first result appeared only in a temporary state and whether the call still landed at the same entry point. Both should be kept together with the caller's version.

If both the first and second results are consistent with the old entry point, the index can include the caller's confirmation in this batch. If the first is consistent but the second changes, stop at this batch for now. If the new entry point errors while the old entry point does not, likewise stop at this batch. If the caller says the results differ but only an edited screenshot remains, with no input and output from before migration, that is not enough to continue to the next batch. The missing item is the original material; do not replace it with a verbal judgment that migration is complete.

When the replacement location can only be inferred from a similar name, retain the old entry point in the index and write the replacement location as pending verification. Similar names are not enough to prove that the call chains are the same; merging it prematurely would leave the caller that is actually still in use without a recovery path. Apply the same handling to an object for which only a directory was found and no call record was found.

```text
First result is comparable, and the second also lands at the same location
    └─ Retain caller confirmation and prepare the next batch

New entry point errors / second result differs / original input is missing
    └─ Stop at the current batch and return to the old entry point for recheck

The old entry point cannot be reused either
    └─ Retain the existing outputs and gaps on both sides; do not change the next batch
```

When a recheck through the old entry point fails, the recovery action must not be recorded as successful. What must be retained here is: which entry point cannot be reused, whether the original input is still available, and which results have already been recorded. If the missing item is the exit location, restore the exit location first and then assess the result difference; if the missing item is caller confirmation, the replacement location is still in trial. Successfully restoring the old entry point only shows that the old path can still serve as a comparison baseline; it does not show that the replacement location can already replace it.

## Batch Records and Related Cards

The return record for ALRB-007 originally retained only the "on-duty person" and a missing section for the exit entry point. The exit entry point was added later, and the exit code still requires further verification. The index therefore treats the exit location and recheck input as one set of records: someone taking over a work item does not mean that the caller already has an executable recovery path. This card is used to review this gap; it does not replace the specific batch in the index.

ALRB-009 once left a rollback check. Here it is understood as an actual review of the old path: the trial record and rollback record are retained together, neither the failed sample is deleted nor is it merged into a successful batch. When the old entry point needs to be used again, start with the input and version retained for this caller before migration, rather than taking output that already passed in another batch.

ALRB-002 was later canceled because a routine task in the core module already covered it. This historical status only means that the separate check is no longer continuing; it cannot be used to infer that all callers of `copying-client-integration` have completed migration. Each row in the index must still be updated based on the actual entry point and confirmation result. ALRB-016 is used to find the users still using `adj-copying`; after finding them, add the entry point, batch, and result; if none are found, leave the search scope instead of writing the empty result as "no users."

Related cards only serve as entry points into the verification records: ALRB-002, ALRB-007, ALRB-009, ALRB-016. The specific migration status is still determined by the caller's row in the index, because a card may retain only the cancellation, return, rollback, or lookup action from that time and cannot replace the comparison between the old path and the replacement location.

## Criteria for Retiring the Old Path

For a caller Fang Ke to stop maintaining its old path, all three conditions must be met: the replacement location can be located in the index; the caller has confirmed its own result; and historical queries can still return to the original entry point and the records from before migration. If any one of the three is missing, retain the old entry point, batch, and unconfirmed marker. What is retired is this caller's old path, not the old name in the entire index.

When multiple callers share one old entry point, complete their respective batches separately first. Confirmation of migration for one object affects only its own entry; if other objects can still enter through the old entry point, continue to retain their inputs, versions, and recovery locations. Keeping the old records this way is not delayed cleanup; it ensures that a caller still in use has somewhere to return when a difference appears at the replacement location.

When checking the index for the final time, first verify whether each "migrated" entry can still answer four questions: Where did it originally enter from? Where did this batch send it? Which input and version were used for comparison? Where should it be restored if the results differ? Return entries that cannot answer these questions to pending verification; do not use a later directory structure to fill in the historical state.

# Postmortem: Caller Integration Records Not Merged

This incident was not simply a page rename. adj-copying had placed the current versions of two revisions behind a single entry point: readers saw one location, but in reality they needed to compare two records from different stages. The entry point remained accessible, but it did not explain the differences between the two records, the time context each preserved, or which one the callers had actually adopted.

The first thing exposed was that the YAML loader did not match the old record. At the time, the evidence could only show that "the content had changed"; it could not explain why. After recovery, rule authoring could continue to be used. This only means that the usable path was restored; it does not mean the two revisions had been merged, and even less does it imply that all callers had returned to the same record. The reason for the Ansible content changes and their adoption scope remain undetermined.

## Earliest Preserved Evidence

Early notes described the issue as "two revisions combined." This preserved the general direction, but did not leave enough information to explain why the two environments produced different current results or which actions had actually run. The first review found only `docs/adj-copying/incidents/COPYING-caller integration two-version records not merged.md`, so the original input and the entry-point version from that time were not cleared.

This was where further retries stopped. It was not because the root cause had been found, but because retrying would overwrite the visible difference caused by mixing the entry points one more time; once only the post-retry state remained, it would no longer be possible to compare what the old and current records each described. This decision preserved the objects that could be reviewed later, but did not fill in the missing time points, nor did it automatically make the observation from the YAML loader at that time the cause.

The only sequence that could be written down at the time was: first, the YAML loader was seen to diverge from the old record; next, the original entry point was preserved; finally, "can continue to be used" was separated from "we know why." The missing time points remain blank; unrecorded actions cannot be written as established facts just to complete the timeline.

## Timeline That Emerged Later

Subsequent records made the impact boundary somewhat more specific and also overturned the initial tendency to attribute the issue directly to the YAML loader.

| Time point | Observed evidence left behind | Judgment possible at the time |
|---|---|---|
| 2025-12-30 | The relevant actions were classified as release-type records | Classification only shows which category the records were placed in; it cannot be treated as a recovery result. |
| 2026-01-01 | The expiration action had passed, but the exit entry point had not entered the queue | The green status covered only the expiration action; it does not show that the exit entry point had been processed. |
| 2026-01-02 | The exit entry point was still absent from the queue records | The missing item must be preserved separately and cannot yet be attributed to the YAML loader. |
| 2026-01-05 | The two environments had different current results, and the commands had not yet been found | The result from one environment cannot explain all callers. |
| 2026-01-06 | The commands for the two environments were still being filled in | Preserve the different current results first; do not guess the missing commands. |
| 2026-01-26 | A sample was attached to the record | There was now comparison input, but no complete list of adopters. |

There are two kinds of "recovery" that are easy to conflate here. One is that the rule authoring path for continued use is no longer blocked at the original failure point; the other is that the relationship between the two revisions has been clarified. The existing evidence supports only the former. The missing exit entry point in the queue is likewise a fact from the evidence; seeing a green status later cannot rewrite it as all related actions having completed successfully.

The records from ALRB-004 state this more narrowly: the temporary owner handled only the expiration action and did not write long-term implications on behalf of COPYING · caller integration. The expiration action passed its time point, while the exit entry point was not queued; the two facts must be preserved separately. Merging them into "already recovered" would erase the missing item needed for continued review later.

## Retracted Attribution

The YAML loader was initially suspected because it was the first thing that differed from the old record. This suspicion could explain the change in visible content, but not why the two environments had different current results, nor why the exit entry point had not entered the queue. After the entry point, environment results, and queue records were separated, the incident had at least two parts: one was that the two revisions shared the current entry point; the other was that the queue records for some actions were incomplete.

The two parts could occur at the same time, but the existing evidence did not prove that either caused the other. Therefore, the judgment that "the YAML loader caused the entire caller integration regression" was retracted. It remains a local observation from the initial review, but is no longer the root cause confirmed on this page. Similarly, the rule profile, Jinja expression, Lintable, and offline CLI that appeared in the old record were only points reached while reviewing the original evidence; they did not acquire any new causal status.

"Ansible content remains normal" can likewise only narrow the scope to the path that had been compared at the time. It cannot be generalized to mean that all callers are normal, much less that the adoption scope has been determined. Once the two environments showed different current results, the former method of inferring overall status from a single path was no longer valid.

## Record Splitting and Retention

The handling proposed by ALRB-006 was to split two copying-client-integration entries by revision without overwriting the old link. This addresses the problem of mixed presentation at the entry point; it does not claim that the two histories have become the same version. The old link should remain available for lookup; otherwise, readers could see only the split results and would not understand why they needed to be separated this time.

ALRB-011 required keeping the navigation entry for the current revision while removing explanatory text that could not be traced back. This change narrowed the promise made by the entry point: navigation can help locate the original record, but explanations must lead back to actual evidence. The entry point can no longer use an unsupported "current" narrative to make a judgment on behalf of two revisions.

ALRB-013 subsequently removed the navigation for the stale current entry point, but the original "COPYING · caller integration two-version records not merged" record and date remain available for lookup. Removing navigation is not deleting the incident history; it only prevents the old entry point from continuing to disguise two stages as one undifferentiated current state. The adjacent DOC-32 can be viewed as a migration index; this page still records only this incident in which two versions were not merged.

The attached sample provides a concrete input for later comparison. It can help determine whether a review is dealing with the same type of material, but it cannot replace environment commands, nor can one sample establish the adoption status of all callers. The commands for the two environments are still pending in the record, so this page does not fabricate an execution sequence from screenshots or the last line of output.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[revision A] --> E[same current entry point]
    B[revision B] --> E
    E --> Y[YAML loader compared with old record]
    Y --> C{Are the current results in the two environments the same}
    C -- different --> S[retain differences and original input]
    C -- same --> Q[check queue records]
    S --> Q
    Q --> X{Did the exit entry point enter the queue}
    X -- no --> U[retain missing item]
    X -- yes --> R[still need to distinguish recovery from cause]
```

The same current entry point in the diagram is the starting point of the incident, not a recommendation to merge the two histories again. During review, first confirm which revision the entry point refers to, then examine the current result left by the corresponding environment, and finally check the queue. If any step is missing, it cannot be filled in with the result from the other environment. In particular, the green status in the queue can show only the actions it actually covered; it cannot replace the execution record for the exit entry point.

## Recovery Assessment

The original entry-point version and original input remain in `docs/adj-copying/incidents/COPYING-caller integration two-version records not merged.md`. This avoids letting the post-recovery state overwrite the history as the only version, and keeps "the path can continue to be used" separate from "the relationship between the two revisions has been resolved."

The actual change after recovery was that rule authoring was no longer blocked by this incident. The parts that were neither restored nor confirmed include whether the two revisions have been separated at all entry points, why the different environments produced different current results, and the scope of the Ansible content changes. Keeping these unconfirmed items in the incident record is more useful than flattening them into a single final green status.

The boundary of the temporary takeover has also been recorded: the expiration action can be handled, but the temporary owner does not fill in long-term implications. This boundary explains why, when the exit entry point is absent from the queue records, this page records only the missing item and does not assume a subsequent action for it. If an adopter is outside the compatibility boundary of copying-client-integration, this page does not infer its result from that fact.

## Still Unresolved

- Why the exit entry point did not enter the queue remains unconfirmed.
- Whether the difference in current results between the two environments was caused by the two revisions sharing an entry point remains unconfirmed.
- The scope of the changes to `Ansible content`, and which callers actually adopted which version, remain unconfirmed.
- Whether the attached sample and the results from the two environments can form part of the same comparison cycle still requires the commands to be filled in.

ALRB-004, ALRB-006, ALRB-011, and ALRB-013 preserve different aspects of this review: the expiration action and exit entry point, revision splitting, removal of unsupported explanations, and removal of stale navigation. They cannot substitute for one another. If command results from the same entry point and the same environment become available later, add them to this record; until then, the original evidence, different current results, and unconfirmed items remain preserved side by side.

# Dependency Audit Entry-Point Migration Index

This index is still referenced by old links. It only collects the legacy entry points, replacement locations, and known callers around modules-supply-boundary: the dependency sources are formed by license and security, while the adoption scope and retirement responsibility remain in their original records. Explanations that could not be traced back remain old claims; the appearance of a new location in the index must not be used to rewrite them as completed migrations.

The entry point is still `docs/adj-modules/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. After opening it, first find the material pointed to by the legacy entry point, then find the replacement location under the same item. Even if other pages have similar names, that is not evidence that the two sides have been merged. This records index relationships; the surrounding projects' own context, schedules, and maintenance details remain in their respective materials.

## How to add an entry

For a migration, first restore beside the legacy entry point the then-current modules-supply-boundary, the current entry point, and the first visible current revision. The gap identified by ALRC-012 is that these three items had once become separated: records organized later may look complete, but they do not show what the state was before the failure. If the original material can no longer be found, leave the gap and the old tense in the entry; do not fill it with newer explanations.

The minimum index format is "legacy entry point / replacement location / caller / adoption scope / retirement responsibility." The caller field should list only a party confirmed to still be using it; leaving it blank is better than merging in a similar name. Adoption scope is not the directory's coverage; it is the scope in which actual users have accepted the replacement location. Retirement responsibility is not the same as deleting a link: only when the old record can still be read and the replacement location can still be used does it make sense to gradually end maintenance of the old path.

```text
Links and original records in the legacy entry point
          │ retain, still searchable
          ▼
Current-entry-legacy-entry migration index
          │ add replacement locations for confirmed callers
          ▼
Replacement location

Rollback: affected callers ──────► legacy entry point
```

The arrows in the diagram do not indicate a one-time cutover sequence. The legacy entry point can remain, and the new location can be trialed; what needs to change is the entry point followed by a specific caller. When no caller has been confirmed in the index, the replacement location can only be labeled a candidate location; it cannot replace the adoption description in the old entry.

## Trial and rollback

During the trial, change only one confirmed caller. Before making the change, preserve the original material and current revision; after the change, record the first result seen by that caller. If the new result cannot be matched to the original material, do not replace it with output organized later. ALRC-008 requires a second colleague to reproduce the issue only by following the original steps, with gaps written directly beside the steps; therefore, do not start a separate, seemingly coherent procedure for the same migration.

An old record once treated "a replacement location already exists in the index" as a sign that the migration was close to complete. That assessment no longer applies, but it is retained here because it explains why some legacy entry points already have new links while callers have not yet migrated. A replacement location only indicates that somewhere to go exists; it does not indicate that the adoption scope has changed or that retirement responsibility has been taken over.

Another old practice was to change the legacy entry point to a one-way redirect once the new location was readable. That loses the rollback path and makes it impossible for later readers to find the original dependency source. Existing entries retain the legacy entry point's readability; if the new location has problems, first point the affected callers back to the legacy entry point, then leave the trial's version and first visible result beside the original entry. Do not delete the replacement location, and do not rewrite a failed attempt as a successful cutover.

When rolling back, first check whether the caller actually switched to the replacement location. Callers that have not switched do not need to be redirected again; after a switched caller is restored to the legacy entry point, the adoption scope remains as recorded originally. Whether to also restore the adoption description in the old record was unresolved in the old version, and the index does not make a new judgment on its behalf.

## Chronology added later

A review of ALRC-007 found that the execution record was dated earlier than the "current result." The original ordering cannot show what happened in between, so the related entries must not be backfilled from the final result. The only thing that can be added with certainty is the "last confirmable state before failure"; everything else remains unknown. ALRC-010's instruction to fill in one step backward from the current entry refers to this action, not to fabricating a continuous record.

After ALRC-009, retain the old assessment and the new result side by side. The old paragraph may state the point in time to which it applied, and the new observation can be appended afterward; do not overwrite the original paragraph with the new assessment. When a single-item confirmation is received, change only the corresponding field. The records in ALRC-011 therefore did not also change the adoption scope or retirement responsibility; each still requires support from its own material.

This index has not yet confirmed all callers item by item. Legacy entry points, replacement locations, and caller relationships that have been located remain here; entries that could not be traced back remain stale. ALRC-007, ALRC-008, ALRC-009, ALRC-010, ALRC-011, and ALRC-012 can be used to return to their respective addenda, but cannot replace the missing original context.

This index still keeps separate records for the old entry point, trial entry point, and rollback entry point. The original version tied `release cache` and `Ansible content` into a single stable path; during the actual cleanup, the failure exits for the two segments were different, so don't use the green result after the old line succeeded to overwrite the trial line's first record.

Trial entry  rule profile ──> Ansible content
                         │
                         └── Roll back to release cache on mismatch

- If the new and old results are the same, keep the old entry until the next artifact window, then record that the caller has migrated.

The Northstar Platform review did not treat the "change window" as a ready-made alternative entry point. # Public Entry Point Maintenance Decision Record

This record preserves the trade-offs made during one round of public entry point maintenance. People later referred back to it not because the entry point's name was enough to explain how the rules were organized, but because it separately recorded "where to keep entering" and "when this route could be retired." That distinction still explains why the entry point was not changed immediately at the time, but it should not be treated as a description of the entry point today.

The subject was the team's public entry point under Northstar Platform. At the start of the discussion, the entry point was treated as a cleanup item on the jinja-rule side: since the rules side would change, it seemed the entry point should be narrowed at the same time. Another view was that the public entry point was first a coordination surface. While existing calls, adjacent checks, and review practices still ran through it, tidy internal naming alone was not enough to decide whether the entry point should stay.

The meeting materials required a record of the actual impact, the coordinator, and the legacy entry point that could be retired. The assessment looked first at reproducible public calls, then at adjacent counterexamples, and finally checked the confirmed parts against frozen repository materials. Inferences not grounded in those materials were not included in the decision at the time. This sequence only limited what could be said in this round; it did not fix the entry point permanently.

Two options were on the table.

- **Keep the existing jinja-rule entry point.** Callers could still complete their reviews through the original path, and differences could first be brought back to the same place for comparison. The cost was that the entry point's name temporarily carried a broader meaning than the rule implementation, and later readers might mistake it for a long-term placement.
- **Adjust the entry point immediately and set an adjustment window.** The boundary would narrow sooner, and the new maintenance notes would be shorter. The cost was that public calls still under review would have to change routes first; why the legacy entry point still existed and when it would be retired would also need a separate explanation.

This round adopted the first option: keep the existing jinja-rule entry point and explicitly identify it as a legacy entry point that could be retired. Keeping it did not mean the internal relationships among the rules had been settled, nor that the later migration had been canceled. It only avoided cutting off the shared lookup path before the call set and counterexamples had been fully collected.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Existing jinja-rule entry point] --> B[Public call review]
    B --> C[Adjacent counterexamples]
    C --> D[Frozen repository materials]
    D --> E[Keep: legacy entry point that can be retired]
    F[Adjustment window] --> G[Call set awaiting confirmation]
    G --> E
```

The decision had concrete effects at the time. Existing calls did not have to switch immediately, and reviews could continue through the original entry point; adjacent issues could first be compared on the same coordination surface, without announcing a new point of entry for every small change; the entry point's name could no longer be treated as the sole clue to where it belonged. The coordinator's job was to bring scattered call differences back into the discussion, not to make migration commitments in advance for every kind of call.

A later review corrected the broader wording in v1. "The entry point is still in use" could only establish that not all public calls had left the old path at the time. It could not establish that every kind of call depended on jinja-rule, much less that the existing entry point was the only entry point. This correction did not change the decision to keep it, but it narrowed the scope in which that decision could be cited. If the old text's "just keep it" wording was read as a long-term principle, that reading went beyond the original assessment.

The option not adopted remains recorded here: adjust the entry point first, then add compatibility notes. It was not proven wrong, but three prerequisites were missing at the time: which public calls needed the legacy entry point, which adjacent counterexamples would lose comparability if the entry point changed, and when the coordinator could announce its retirement. Changing the entry point before filling in those details would leave explanations for the new entry point, the legacy entry point, and the temporary fallback all at once. It would not reduce the maintenance burden.

DOC-44 preserves partial clues from the switchover handoff. This page preserves why the public entry point was not retired first, before the switchover became an established fact. The two pages can point to each other, but neither replaces the other: the handoff materials concern how the later takeover happened; this page only preserves the options compared at the time, the costs of the option not adopted, and the condition that the legacy entry point could be retired.

The retirement conditions were not developed into a schedule at the time. A review sufficient to cover the differences among public calls was needed first, followed by confirmation that adjacent counterexamples remained comparable, before it would be appropriate to revisit an entry point adjustment. This gap is part of the original record; it shows that the decision deferred an adjustment rather than providing a complete migration plan.

The content on this page that remains useful today is therefore narrow: the public entry point was kept, it was kept with retirement conditions attached, and the decision at the time rejected substituting an unconfirmed call set for evidence. It does not provide the entry point's present status, nor does it promise that jinja-rule will continue to be the public name in the future.

# Postmortem: Deviation in Public-Entry Maintenance

During the maintenance window for the team's shared public entry point, the visible result did not match the original plan. When the issue was first found, the team on site did not treat the entry point remaining visible as a completion signal; instead, it recorded "entry visible" and "result matches the plan" separately. The original execution record was retained. It confirms that the deviation occurred and that temporary recovery took place, but it does not support inferring that any particular step was the cause.

## What Happened During the Window

- After the window began, the team maintained the shared public entry point according to the original plan. The expectation at the time was that the result shown by the entry point would change accordingly once processing was complete.
- The first check found that the visible result had not appeared as expected. The team initially recorded the situation as a switch-order deviation. This described only the gap observed at the time and was not supported by enough records to confirm the root cause.
- During coordination, the coordinator recorded the actual impact that had already surfaced and retained the old entry so it could be withdrawn. This kept temporary recovery from consuming the only rollback path and avoided recording unquantified impact as no impact.
- After temporary recovery, the entry point returned to a state where processing could continue. The recovery resolved the direct deviation within the window, but it did not show which step in the original plan had failed to take effect, nor did it prove that the earlier sequence assessment was correct.

## Judgments Recorded at the Time

The original plan treated the shared public entry point as something that could be completed in a single operation. The on-site record later added a narrower distinction: the entry point being visible indicates only the access state after recovery; whether the result it presents matches the original plan still requires checking against the original execution record. The window record did not collapse these two facts into a single "recovered" conclusion.

The actual impact had also not been quantified by the end of the window. The record preserves only the observed deviation, the old entry retained during coordination, and the items still awaiting inspection after temporary recovery. This wording preserves the old framing at the time, which attributed the issue to switch order, so a later review can see why the team prioritized recovery; it should not be treated as a causal explanation for subsequent maintenance.

## Open Items

The original record does not provide reproducible trigger conditions and is insufficient to attribute the deviation to a single processing step. At the end of the window, what could be confirmed was temporary recovery and that the old entry could still be withdrawn; the cause remained unresolved, and the scope of the actual impact had not been confirmed.

JinjaRule.matchtask returns either a MatchError or false; only AnsibleLintRule.matchtasks defines the boundary of the flat MatchError list. _enrich_matcherror_with_task_details receives (match, task), preserves the task identity, and produces Task/Handler: details. ansiblelint.config.get_version_warning reads only replaceable CACHE_DIR/latest.json; guess_install_method is the installation-method hook. A missing, empty, corrupt, non-object, or incomplete cache returns an empty message; valid metadata is not invalidated by an expired mtime. It does not access the network or create or rewrite the cache. The same version returns an empty message, even if the installation-method hook provides an upgrade command. This function returns a string; --offline --version use the same read-only cache strategy and end with status 0. Lintable.data infers an unspecified kind from tasks or rules before rule scheduling. NameRule handles task_name_prefix and name[missing], name[casing], name[play], name[prefix], and name[template]. The tag_stats of App.count_results maps valid tags to TagStats objects, exposes count, warning, tag, profile, order, and the associated_tags property, and uses an independent summary on every call. In a new summary, failures/warnings is 0 and the mapping is empty; on an entry's first match, count=1, tag is the valid tag, and associated_tags comes from the rule category. warning is determined by the valid tag, rule ID, or the intersection of the category and warn_list. Before sorting, order=0 and profile is empty. Equivalent property-object implementations are allowed.
versions.change_summary: Publish observable return shapes, version-cache boundaries, and statistics entry types

Current public API contract (ansible-lint-cumulative-20260926-r5): JinjaRule.check_whitespace(text, key) returns (formatted, details, tag); for no change, the original text, empty details, and spacing; for an invalid template, empty formatted, diagnostic details, and invalid. JinjaRule.matchtask returns a MatchError or false value, and only AnsibleLintRule.matchtasks is the boundary for the flat MatchError list; _enrich_matcherror_with_task_details receives (match, task), preserves the task identity, and generates Task/Handler: details. ansiblelint.config.get_version_warning only reads the replaceable CACHE_DIR/latest.json; guess_install_method is the installation-method hook; ansiblelint.config.__version__ is the replaceable current-version string; get_version_warning reads its current value on every call. A missing, empty, corrupt, non-object, or missing-field cache returns an empty hint; valid metadata does not become invalid because its mtime expires; there is no network access, and the cache is not created or rewritten; the same version returns an empty hint, even when the installation-method hook provides an upgrade command. When a newer cached release applies, the returned notice also includes the nonempty upgrade command supplied by the installation-method hook. This function returns a string; --offline --version uses the same read-only cache strategy and ends with status 0. YAML without an explicit kind infers the type from the parsed content: a list item containing hosts and tasks is a playbook, while one containing hosts and rules is a rulebook. The first read of Lintable.kind after construction must return the inferred result; there is no need to read Lintable.data first or execute the rules; inference at construction time or lazy inference through the kind property is allowed. NameRule is responsible for task_name_prefix and name[missing], name[casing], name[play], name[prefix], and name[template]. The tag_stats of App.count_results maps valid tags to TagStats objects, exposes the count, warning, tag, profile, order, and associated_tags attributes, and uses an independent summary on every call. The failures/warnings of a new summary is 0, and the mapping is empty; for an entry's first hit, count=1, tag is the valid label, and associated_tags comes from the rule category; warning is determined by the valid tag, rule ID, or the intersection of the category and warn_list; before sorting, order=0, and profile is empty. Equivalent attribute-object implementations are allowed.

Profile runtime contract: min, basic, moderate, safety, shared, and production inherit successively in the listed order; production inherits shared. min has no parent; omitting extends, using null, or using another equivalent empty value representing no parent is allowed; an empty mapping can serve as the root description. CLI --profile preserves the single-element selection and excludes rules that do not belong to that profile or its ancestors before execution; it must not execute first and then delete diagnostics. min enables only fatal checks such as loading, parsing, and syntax checks; basic adds name, jinja, and basic-format checks, and later profiles inherit these checks. The complete rule grouping is in the table on the same page; rules not yet present in the table are not required to be added in this round.

| Profile | Parent | Direct rule membership |
| --- | --- | --- |
| min | (none) | internal-error, load-failure, parser-error, syntax-check |
| basic | min | command-instead-of-module, command-instead-of-shell, deprecated-bare-vars, deprecated-command-syntax, deprecated-local-action, deprecated-module, inline-env-var, key-order, literal-compare, jinja, no-jinja-when, no-tabs, partial-become, playbook-extension, role-name, schema, name, var-naming, yaml |
| moderate | basic | name-templated, name-imperative, name-capital, no-shorthand, spell-var-name |
| safety | moderate | git-latest, hg-latest, package-latest, risky-file-permissions, risky-octal, risky-shell-pipe |
| shared | safety | ignore-errors, layout, meta-incorrect, meta-no-info, meta-no-tags, meta-video-links, meta-version, meta-unsupported-ansible, no-changed-when, no-changelog, no-handler, no-relative-paths, max-block-depth, max-tasks, unsafe-loop |
| production | shared | avoid-dot-notation, disallowed-ignore, fqcn-builtins, import-task-no-when, meta-no-dependencies, single-entry-point, use-loop |


The representation flexibility in this revision applies to all callers. For other conditions and the specific boundaries concerning names, YAML, and rule loading, check with the owner of the corresponding card; the public APIs of DOC-49 take precedence over old drafts, and the owner is responsible for the current details of their card.

A single-element profile is the configuration selection returned by get_config and used at runtime; the intermediate result of get_cli_parser may be a string and is then normalized during configuration.
versions.change_summary: Clarify pre-run profile selection, the inheritance rules table, and equivalent root representations; keep the existing ownership split for all other details.
